chapters.summary: Council staff welcomes attendees to the Committee on Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation hearing, instructs attendees to silence devices, explains that witnesses must fill out slips with the sergeant at arms, and notes no one may approach the dais.
chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and explains witness procedures

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please silence all electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you would like to testify, you must fill out a witness slip with one of the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Just a reminder, no one may approach the dais at any time.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, we are ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Gale Brewer convenes the hearing titled 'Access to Government and the Mamdani Administration Civic Engagement Efforts,' welcomes DORIS, the Office of Mass Engagement, the Campaign Finance Board, the Conflict of Interest Board, and colleagues including Council Member Wilson and the Public Advocate.
chapters.title: Chair Brewer opens hearing on access to government and civic engagement

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm Gail Brewer, Chair of the Committee on Government Operations, State and Federal Legislation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want to thank everyone for joining us today for the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're calling it Access to Government and the Mandami Administration Civic Engagement Efforts.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I would certainly like to welcome individuals from the Department of Records and Information Services, DORIS.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's my favorite agency.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Nobody else likes it as much as I do.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The Office of Mass Engagement, the Campaign Finance Board, and the Conflict of Interest Board, the public, and council colleagues who have joined us today.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think Council Member Wilson is here, and we're going to hear from the wonderful public advocate in a minute.

chapters.summary: Brewer describes the four preconsidered bills: two sponsored by Minority Leader Carr on prohibiting candidates in government-funded third-party communications and reporting on third-party public communications, one by Council Member Feliz on disclosures for government-funded communications, and one by Council Member Wong on campaign finance disclosures for online content.
chapters.title: Brewer outlines four preconsidered bills before the committee

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In addition to oversight today, we will be hearing four pre-considered bills.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One which is sponsored by Minority Leader Carr in relation to prohibiting candidates from appearing in certain government-funded third-party communications during an election campaign.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Another one sponsored by Minority Leader Carr.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: by Minority Leader Carr in relation to reporting on third-party public communications.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And another one sponsored by Councilmember Feliz in relation to requiring disclosures on third-party public communication paid for with government resources.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And finally, one sponsored by Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In relation to requiring campaign finance disclosures in content posted on internet websites, digital applications, and social media platforms,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and directing the Campaign Finance Board to issue guidance regarding the disclosure, record keeping, and reporting requirements applicable to such content.

chapters.summary: Brewer says government use of influencers is a good thing for public health, elections, and tourism, but notes inconsistency among agencies on disclosure wording and hashtags, citing Health and Hospitals and the Campaign Finance Board as examples of good practice.
chapters.title: Brewer explains government use of influencers and inconsistency in disclosures

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Government use of influencers has become the norm, and that's a good thing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Influencers are a good thing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But governments use influencers to increase awareness on public health issues, a good thing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Boost election participation, that's needed.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Attract tourists, among other things.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There's nothing wrong with using influences, and they can actually help government officials reach populations that are difficult to reach through traditional media.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Not everybody can watch New York One like me.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Government agencies in New York City primarily use social media influencer in two different ways.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: First,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Agencies work with influencers to create targeted campaigns.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And one of the first examples of a success.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: use of social media, influences in a public awareness campaign, health and hospitals, use them to encourage New Yorkers to get tested and then to get vaccinated against COVID.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Recently, the Campaign Finance Board, through its NYC Votes initiative,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: partnered with influencers to increase voter turnout and civic engagement.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Health and hospitals and the campaign finance board generally include, those campaigns include some type of disclosure that they are paid for by the city.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This is not, however, the case with all city agencies, and that's the issue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There is no consistency among agencies on the wording of the disclosures, what kind of hashtags, etc.

chapters.summary: Brewer cites a Columbia Journalism Review report by Dr. Anya Schiffrin on an invite-only Signal group used by the mayor's communications team to share talking points with influencers, raising concerns about auto-delete features and compliance with city document retention rules.
chapters.title: Brewer describes mayor's Signal group and document retention concerns

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The second way that the mayor in particular uses social media is more novel and very effective.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: At the end of the last month, a Columbia journalism review by the very great Dr.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Anya Shifreya reported, she reported on the use, and she'll be here today to talk about it,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: of an invite-only signal group used by the mayor's communication team to share updates, talking points, and clips to a selected group of social media influencers.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The Signal messaging app allows users to auto-delete messages.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's how Signal works.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And it is not clear in what

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: cases of this feature was active.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The signal service don't keep copies of messages.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So we want to ensure that the mayor's team is following the city's document retention rules when using the app, and that's called archiving.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm an archive nut.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just want people to know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There also appears to be at least some overlap between the influencers who are paid to promote agency campaigns and those on the mayor's signal distribution list.

chapters.summary: Brewer explains the mayor created the Office of Mass Engagement on his second day, absorbing the Community Affairs Unit, Public Engagement Unit, ethnic media office, faith-based partnerships, and NYC Service, and states the hearing will examine FOIL and archiving issues.
chapters.title: Brewer introduces Office of Mass Engagement and hearing goals

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In addition to finding out about the mayor's use of the social media influencers and the signal app, we are also going to hear from the mayor's newly created Office of Mass Engagement.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: On Justice's second day in office, the mayor created this office, which, according to the mayor, was intended to create a connection between City Hall and everyday New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This office replaced the Community Affairs Unit, the Public Engagement Unit, the Mayor's Office of Ethnic and Community Media,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The Office of Faith-Based and Community Partnerships and the New York City Service were all placed under this new office as well, although I think one of them may have moved over to communications.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: While the work of OME is consistent with the work of the Public Engagement Unit, which now reports to it, it has a greater emphasis on connecting with New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and engaging them in governmental processes while also making sure that they are aware of their rights as New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: New Yorkers need to know what their benefits are, and this office helps to do that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We would like to find out more how this office works and how it differs from the mayor's outreach during the election campaign.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We also want to hear about any legislation that they might suggest on this topic.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And obviously we want to know about FOIL, and we want to know about archiving from DARIS.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Those are the issues that I desperately care about.

chapters.summary: Brewer thanks Government Ops staff Johari Frazier, Erica Cohen, and Sigmo Hamid, and her staff Shula Puder and Cynthia Hornig, notes the presence of Minority Leader Carr, Council Member Wong, and Council Member Ariola on Zoom, and invites opening statements.
chapters.title: Brewer thanks staff and invites opening statements

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want to thank the following council staff for their work on this hearing, from Government Ops, Johari Frazier, Erica Cohen, and Sigmo Hamid, and from my staff, Shula Puder and Cynthia Hornig,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and everyone who helps make this hearing run smoothly.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think we've also been joined by Minority Leader Carr, Councilmember Wong, and on Zoom, Councilmember Areola.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I don't know if Councilmember Carr, if you want to, or Wong, if you want to make some opening statements.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Carr.

chapters.summary: Carr describes the NYC Creators Announcements Signal group with over 200 influencers sharing daily talking points, criticizes Amelia Rowland's statement dismissing communication norms, and argues the encrypted disappearing-message app evades record-keeping laws.
chapters.title: Minority Leader Carr condemns mayor's Signal group and influencer operation

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Brewer, for holding this important hearing today, and thank you to Speaker Menon for her leadership on this issue.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: When Zoran Mamdani rode his social media stardom to the Merrill D last year, I think we all understood that there was a real paradigm shift in the way politicians engage with the public.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: That was made even more clear when the mayor brought his campaign communication apparatus to City Hall.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I don't think we understood the extent of that change until a recent report by the Initiative for Policy Dialogue at Columbia University mentioned by Chair Brewer.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: that revealed that the mayor's office has been operating a signal group chat called NYC Creators Announcements with over 200 social media influencers.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: In this group, the report found that the mayor's office shares daily talking points, videos, and other ways to spread favorable messaging about the mayor and the administration.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: They are also invited to events and offered access to city officials.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: In response to this revelation, Amelia Rowland, who as the mayor's director of new media, runs this and influenced her campaign,

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: said, quote, at a moment of profound distrust in politics, our job is not to preserve decades-old communication norms or protect the gatekeepers who once controlled access to public information, end quote.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Indeed, there is a profound mistrust in politics today.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: But that mistrust is only intensified when city officials conduct business with outside entities using an encrypted messaging app with disappearing messages, purposely designed to evade public scrutiny and laws that require record keeping.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And when these new quote-unquote gatekeepers buy their access to the mayor by amplifying his propaganda.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It's also somewhat ironic, given Ms.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Rowland's statement, that the so-called legacy media she seemed to deride was the one that revealed this repetitious partnership.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: What makes this new communication strategy more alarming than others is the fact that these influencers who have built up their own brands because of the perception that they are genuine.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: and authentic are able to convince the public that these are not coordinated and yet often are and paid for as a message and objective of those so-called honest views.

chapters.summary: Carr cites a New York Times AI analysis finding most influencer videos about the administration were positive, notes FTC disclosure rules and campaign finance requirements, and says his legislation would require disclosure of who collaborates with the mayor's office, the subject matter, and payments.
chapters.title: Carr explains FTC and campaign finance loopholes his bills would close

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: According to the New York Times, an artificial intelligence analysis of more than a dozen Instagram influencers who work with the mayor's team found that of 178 videos related to the administration, the overwhelming majority were positive.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: The Federal Trade Commission has laws to prevent deceptive advertisement, including new rules for disclosure for social media influencers.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: There are also campaign finance rules that require disclosure of payments.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: To anyone who is working on behalf of a candidate and their committees.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: But there is a big loophole when it comes to this type of relationship between influencers and government entities.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: The legislation we are introducing today aims to close that loophole by requiring the disclosure of these relationships.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It will let us know who is collaborating with the mayor's office and the city agencies, the subject matter of these messages, and whether they are being paid for by the government for such messaging, and if so, how much.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: These are basic guardrails that will protect against misrepresentation and give the public the full picture about the message they are receiving.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong, do you want to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So now then we're going to hear from the public advocate.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams testifies that New Yorkers should understand who is communicating with them and with what resources, noting city social media is branded but third-party communications raise new questions about distinguishing official government messages.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams calls for transparency in government communications

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: My name is Jermaine Williams, Public Advocate of the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I want to thank Chair Brewer and members of the Governmental Operations State and Federal Legislative Committee for holding this hearing and for the opportunity to share the statement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In order to create effective civic engagement, New Yorkers should readily understand who is communicating with them and what capacity and with what resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: City agencies use social media to communicate information about various services, emergencies, and opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The city's own social media policy recognizes that these platforms provide agencies with ways to directly and meaningfully reach constituents and disseminate information about services it may provide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Currently, social media content from NYC agencies is branded as such, and individuals can see that it comes from a government source.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Simultaneously, the ever-changing digital landscape creates new questions about how New Yorkers will continue to be able to distinguish official government communications from communications distributed by third parties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: At its core, government communication should be rooted in transparency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: New Yorkers should know who is communicating with them and where the public resources are being used.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In a moment where deep fakes and misinformation from the highest level of government make a public discernment increasingly difficult, it's even more important than ever here in New York City that we don't just follow every rule for compliance with the government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: but that we build a trust with the public that federal counterparts in Washington, D.C.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Seem intent on destroying.

chapters.summary: Williams cites DORIS's 2025 instant messaging policy requiring retention of messages documenting decisions, actions, or policies, and argues auto-delete features on Signal and WhatsApp violate public records laws and prevent FOIL responses.
chapters.title: Williams warns disappearing messages violate records retention laws

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The New York City Department of Records and Information Services, DORIS, which apparently is the favorite of Gail Brewer,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: 2025 policy on instant electronic messages explicitly states that messages that document decisions, actions, or policies in an office or agency makes must be retained and preserved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The policy further establishes that these offices and agencies must set procedures for gathering these messages, including but not limited to screenshots or exporting data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This raises particular concerns when city employees or agencies use third-party messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Signal with automatic deletion or disappearing message features.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: While these outside applications would be more than appropriate for personal communications, the message delete delegation...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Delegation feature violates public records and data retention laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These vanishing messages prevent government transparency, making public communication unrecoverable for freedom of information or open records requests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Using these apps, even if no official records were deleted, raises questions at minimum in the public, and those are questions that should not need to be answered if the same permissible conversations occurred by other methods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As public servants, I believe it is a best practice to not invite questions of secrecy in the course of doing our jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: There are a number of pieces of legislation from my colleagues, Councilmember Phileas Wong and Carr, that seem to address this.

chapters.summary: Williams says he looks forward to reading the bills from Council Members Feliz, Wong, and Carr, states he doesn't know if the administration did anything wrong, and hopes the administration will assuage concerns about access, particularly for ethnic media.
chapters.title: Williams says he doesn't know if administration did wrong but seeks trust

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I look forward to reading them more deeply and understanding how it will address the concerns we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I also look forward to hearing from the city agencies about all of the stories.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I did want to just make clear, I don't know if the administration has done anything wrong at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I think this is just hearing is also about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I do know in this time period we have to create and be convincing about an atmosphere of trust, particularly in the ever-changing communication AI

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: space and a backdrop of where we hear from small and particularly ethnic-specific media about their lack of access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so I'm hoping today that the administration will assuage some of the concerns that we've heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I couldn't think of a better person to help lead that conversation to council than the current chair, Gabriel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Those are very kind words.

chapters.title: Council staff administers affirmation to administration panelists

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And now I'd like to turn the proceedings over to the community council to administer the oath.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We will now hear from the administration.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Panelists, will you please raise your right hand?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

chapters.summary: Shanta Smith-Cruz, newly appointed Commissioner of the Department of Records and Information Services (DORIS), introduces colleagues Rose Nagel-Indigoyen, Lauren Gilbert, and Sylvia Collar, and notes she is joined by Commissioner Tasha Van Auken of the Office of Mass Engagement.
chapters.title: DORIS Commissioner Shanta Smith-Cruz introduces herself and her team

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Hello, good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Chair Brewer, members of City Council, it's a true pleasure to introduce the work of the Department of Records and Information Services, Describe Policy, Records Management, and Retention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: My name is Shanta Smith-Cruz, and also if you are reading along, this is not a draft, so you can delete that from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I'm the newly appointed commissioner for the Department for Records and Information Services, affectionately known as DORIS, and we appreciate your affection, Chair Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I am joined by my colleagues, Rose Nagel-Indigoyen, Director of Municipal Records, Lauren Gilbert, Director of Municipal Library, behind me, and Sylvia Collar, Director of Municipal Archives, also sitting behind me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I'm also grateful to be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Alongside Commissioner Tasha Van Auken and her colleagues from the Office of Mass Engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: My background is as a writer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: writer, editor, academic librarian, community archivist, faculty member in information science, and native New Yorker.

chapters.summary: Smith-Cruz outlines DORIS's three divisions—municipal archives, municipal library, and municipal records—citing 11.3 million digitized items, 10.5 million historical vital records, 74,000 government publications, and 185,000 cubic feet of records, with 77% requiring preservation work.
chapters.title: Smith-Cruz describes DORIS divisions, collections, and services

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I want to first briefly introduce Doris and its function.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: In accordance with the charter, Doris is organized into three main divisions, the municipal archives, a municipal library,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: and municipal records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Doris provides the public with access to more than 11.3 million digitized items, including historical photographs, maps, and documents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The Historical Vital Records platform provides free online access to 10.5 million high-quality copies of historical birth, death, and marriage records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The Municipal Library hosts the government publications portal, a growing online collection of more than 74,000 reports and publications issued by city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We respond to more than 28,000 reference requests and provide access to approximately

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: 185,000 cubic feet and more than 400 terabytes of historical city records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Along with a collection of more than 400,000 books, government reports, studies, and other publications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Approximately 77% of the archival holdings require preservation work, and we have a conservation unit that oversees the rehousing, conservation treatments, and other specialized methods.

chapters.summary: Smith-Cruz describes the municipal records management division serving 65 government entities, overseeing digital records transition, and managing the city's open records FOIL portal, with City Council slated to onboard within the month.
chapters.title: Smith-Cruz explains records management division and FOIL portal onboarding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The department's municipal records management division develops and administers records management policies,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: operates record storage facilities, provides one-to-one liaison records management services to 65 government entities,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: and we oversee the city's government's transition to digital records management.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We manage the city's open records FOIL portal, which is in process of onboarding all agencies of the city of New York, including city council, who is slated to onboard within the month, so that's really exciting, into open records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: To support records management across the entire city, records management is serviced by records management officers based within each city agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Doris has five records management officer liaisons, one of whom is with me here today, who is the department director.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And we train records management officers and provide them with resources informed by national field standards, and all records management policies are written in collaboration with the law department.

chapters.summary: Smith-Cruz explains the archival principle that not all records are archival, with retention schedules ranging from zero to 99 years or perpetuity, and introduces the May 2025 instant electronic messaging policy developed with the Law Department.
chapters.title: Smith-Cruz explains retention schedules and the 2025 instant messaging policy

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The records management lifecycle contends with a basic archival principle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Not all records are archival.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Instead, we ask, is the record active?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Is the record substantive?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: For how long does it need to be retained?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Does it have historical and enduring value?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Answers to these questions lead the record series retention schedules, which can be as long as 99 years or perpetuity, on average three to eight, maybe 10 years, and as low as a schedule of zero.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Which brings me to instant messaging policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Policies and practices regarding instant messages relate to the May 25, May 2025 policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: This policy was in close consultation with the law department and the office of the chief counsel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Doris updated its policy on instant electronic messaging records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And I brought copies of the policy so that we can read along together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So if one of the guards could help me pass along the document.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: There he goes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I'm a librarian, so I like read-alongs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I didn't take one for myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so when you receive it,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: You'll note that it does state, I don't actually.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: In bold and underline on page two.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Instant electronic messages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Oh, wait, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Okay, on page two in bold and underlined so that it's not hidden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And this policy has actually been posted online since its development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: In May 2025.

chapters.summary: Smith-Cruz reads from the policy stating instant electronic messages are transitory by default with no expectation of retention, but users must transfer substantive content to a format appropriate for long-term storage, and the policy discourages creating substantive instant messages.
chapters.title: Smith-Cruz details transitory versus substantive message rules

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Instant electronic messages are considered transitory by default.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: There is no expectation of retention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: If a user determines the content of a message is substantive and should be maintained, the user is charged with transferring the content to a format more appropriate for long-term storage and use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Under this policy, instant messaging or text messages are treated similarly to a phone call or a conversation at a conference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: By default, such communications are deemed

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: transitory and therefore not subject to retention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But if the content of the message happens to be substantive in connection with city business, then the city employee should move that content to other platforms for retention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The policy also strongly discourages city employees from creating instant electronic messages that are substantive in nature.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: When records are found to be substantive and do have enduring value, they become archival.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The Archives'work in preservation and access considers the changing formats and environments in which New York City government conducts its business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And that brings us to digital solutions and considerations.

chapters.summary: Smith-Cruz says DORIS implemented RecordPoint, used by 31 agencies including the Office of the Mayor to manage 215 million records, but it only maps government-supplied tools; social media posts are archived permanently via Civic Plus/Archive Social covering Facebook, X, Instagram, TikTok, and others.
chapters.title: Smith-Cruz describes RecordPoint and social media archiving tools

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Doris has initiated the city's engagement with the electronic records governance tool, RecordPoint.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: RecordPoint enables agencies to categorize electronic records in accordance with their existing retention schedules and is being implemented across all agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: To date, 31 agencies, including the Office of the Mayor, uses the system, which manages more than 215 million records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: This tool empowers agencies to enforce retention and disposal to their mapped data repositories, properly managing records across their lifecycle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: This tool, however, only maps to government-supplied tools where substantive records are held.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: This is because we as a field have a ways to go before these types of tools are manageable across all types of digital platforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Our policies aim to keep up to date with the 2026 modern day use of various digital tools and platforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: To that end, we must also consider

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: that all digital platforms serve different purposes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: For example, transitory messages in a messaging platform, they operate at a very different speed than a social media post, which is by default considered a publication

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: and has a policy of archival permanence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I didn't bring a copy of our social media policy, but our social media policy states, quote, social media records have a permanent retention and are required to be transferred to the municipal library, end quote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The social media policy was last updated in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: However, Local Law 41 in 2025 expanded the requirement to maintain a publicly accessible and searchable online database that contains all publicly viewable content and metadata shared by a government official's social media account.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We work with OTI to contract with a third-party vendor an archival tool called Civic Plus or Archive Social.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Civic Plus functioned to capture agency archival information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Doris is now able to automate and facilitate this process, supporting the onboarding work of connecting the social media accounts of officials and agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Civic Plus is currently capable of archiving the following platforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Facebook, X, Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, YouTube, Vimeo, Nextdoor, Pinterest, Flickr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: They are aware of the city's interest in Blue Sky, Reddit, and WhatsApp, but cannot provide an estimate of when those platforms might be added.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: If a platform

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: is eventually added, Civic Plus would be able to go back to the start of the account and retroactively harvest all of the content.

chapters.summary: Smith-Cruz states DORIS does not see Council Member Carr's reporting bill as within its jurisdiction, noting DORIS is not asked to report on other agencies' work but can supply the government publications portal as a reporting tool.
chapters.title: Smith-Cruz says Carr's social media bill is outside DORIS jurisdiction

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: As it relates to the bill that was posed by Councilmember Carr, Doris does not see this new process as within the jurisdiction of our work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We are not asked to report on other agencies'work, but as the stewards of the government publications portal, we can supply the tool for reporting that another agency may use to upload within the pre-existing portal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So I'd like to end by grounding us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We are here to be responsive to New York City's open access to government history and records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Our charter mandate is clearly written and does not, for example, ask us to become a reporting agency for non-municipal behaviors, such as what may be being recommended in Carr's social media bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Instead, we operate in service to community, to archival practice, library public service, and to stewarding efficient records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I've provided a lengthy testimony to be as informative as possible to underscore process and practice for our collective aim of transparency through government records, which I hope has been made clear this morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So now I thank you for your attention and welcome your questions and pass the mic to Commissioner Van Aken.

chapters.summary: Tasha Van Auken, Commissioner of the Mayor's Office of Mass Engagement, explains the office was created on the mayor's second day to bring New Yorkers into government, reaching hundreds of thousands on policies, services, extreme weather, and civic participation.
chapters.title: OME Commissioner Tasha Van Auken introduces Office of Mass Engagement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Brewer and the members of the Committee on Governmental Operations for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: My name is Tasha Van Auken, and I'm the Commissioner of the Mayor's Office of Mass Engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Mayor Mamdani established the Office of Mass Engagement on his second day in office out of a belief that good governance requires bringing New Yorkers into the work of government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Since then, we've reached hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers to engage them about new policies, help them navigate city services, support them through extreme weather events, and develop their civic participation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: New Yorkers care a lot about their city, but we're also famously busy people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: It's hard to get informed, get involved, and have a voice when city government seems so opaque and difficult to navigate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: New Yorkers are juggling jobs, kids, caring for elders, and much more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We can't wait for them to come to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We meet New Yorkers where they are to help them access services and participate in the decisions that affect their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: A benefit only helps someone if they know it exists, that they are eligible for it, and understand how to access it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: A public hearing is only truly public if New Yorkers know it is happening, know how to participate, and believe their voice belongs in the room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: OME's job is to demystify government processes and add new pathways for New Yorkers to engage with policies and see the positive impacts of their participation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We connect several long-established offices for civic engagement, like the Public Engagement Unit,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: NYC service and the Civic Engagement Commission with new initiatives to educate and involve New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: we are able to draw on the deep well of knowledge and relationships that these historic engagement offices offer while expanding the ways that New Yorkers can participate in government.

chapters.summary: Van Auken details the Office of Faith-Based Partnerships building relationships at over 120 faith events, interfaith tenant canvasses, and community liaisons supporting cultural events like the African Heritage Reception and staffing parades across all five boroughs.
chapters.title: Van Auken describes faith-based partnerships and community liaison work

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Some of OME's teams include the Office of Faith-Based Partnerships, which fosters reciprocal relationships with New York's diverse faith communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our team of faith liaisons have built relationships at over 120 faith-based events and meetings since OME's inception and facilitated the mayor's presence at nearly half of those events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: These range from visiting houses of worship with the mayor to interfaith and holiday events like the 38th annual Pagwa Parade, Passover at Gracie Mansion, and backpack distribution with the New York Disaster Interfaith Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: To name just a few.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Faith-based partnerships supports roundtables that bring New York's faith communities into deeper engagement with city government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We also hosted three interfaith tenant canvases, one of which was OME's highest attended canvas with nearly 50 attendees, forging a new model for faith-based civic engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our community liaisons bring a range of communities into the work of governance, develop meaningful heritage events that connect the mayorality to the cultural life of our city, and build civic leadership in under-engaged communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: OME community liaisons have visited

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: community-based organizations in all five boroughs, supported the planning of cultural events at Gracie Mansion, like the African Heritage Reception and the Mid-Autumn Festival,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: staffed parades from the West Indian Day Parade to the Mexican Independence Day Parade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: and attended community events on behalf of the mayor's office from the Hong Kong Dragon Boat Festival to the recent Battle of Jollof, which brings the West African community together over food, sport, and culture.

chapters.summary: Van Auken describes the citywide constituent affairs team coordinating responses on deed theft, housing discrimination, and flooding; the emergency response team aiding during snowstorms and floods; and borough organizers attending over 240 community board meetings.
chapters.title: Van Auken outlines constituent affairs, emergency response, and borough organizing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our citywide constituent affairs team coordinates proactive, responsive action to New Yorkers'issues, from deed theft to housing discrimination, trash pickup, flood response, and much more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: For example, Constituent Affairs recently coordinated across multiple agencies to take action to aid a school experiencing recurring flooding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our emergency response team delivers crucial information and support to New Yorkers through snowstorms, wildfire, smoke, and floods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We also provide compassionate touch points and wraparound services to New Yorkers after serious tragedies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our emergency response team organized a coastal zone preparedness call.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Over 150 New Yorkers living in areas most vulnerable to coastal storms received life-saving information about how to prepare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: And our borough organizing team maintains strong relationships with community boards and other longstanding civic partners, while also building new relationships with tenants, resident leaders, community-based organizations, and other neighborhood networks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Borough organizing builds hyper-local relationships to create more ways for New Yorkers to organize around the issues affecting them and engage directly with City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Borough organizers have attended over 240 community board meetings, district service cabinet meetings, borough-wide cabinet meetings,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: one-on-ones with district managers and or chairs, and other ad hoc meetings to build relationships with community boards and dig in on borough-specific issues.

chapters.summary: Van Auken says the events team supported over 30 events attended by 5,800 New Yorkers, the co-governance team helped launch a $3 million child care emergency grant program, and the campaigns team knocked on over 10,000 doors leading to nearly 2,500 organizing conversations.
chapters.title: Van Auken describes events, co-governance, and campaigns teams

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our events team has supported over 30 events in 30 weeks, attended by over 5,800 New Yorkers, from New York City 101s, where New Yorkers get educated on how our government works,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: to events like Pick Up at the People's House and cultural heritage events, where New Yorkers can see their heritage uplifted at City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our co-governance team supports agencies and the administration in building out models for shared accountability with New Yorkers and advocates in policymaking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: For example, they supported the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education on building a co-governance table for child care workers that led to the launch of a $3 million emergency grant program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: specifically in response to the needs and gaps identified by this table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: This is yet another way that OME strives to bring New Yorkers into the work of city government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: The campaigns team empowers the most impacted New Yorkers to participate in the decisions that affect them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: New York City volunteers, led by our staff, have knocked on over 10,000 doors, leading to nearly 2,500 successful organizing conversations with New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: In these conversations, we listened to their concerns, shared information about their rights, and invited them out to educational events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We've seen great success in this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: At the recent bus rider town hall with Mayor Mumdani and the Department of Transportation, 70% of attendees were from zip codes directly impacted by the bus plan.

chapters.summary: Van Auken describes emergency response and faith partnerships emailing heat warnings to 600,000 New Yorkers and translating safety messaging, and the Public Engagement Unit knocking on 10,000 doors and making 40,000 calls to help 11,000 New Yorkers keep SNAP benefits.
chapters.title: Van Auken details interagency collaboration during heatwaves and SNAP outreach

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our teams also work extremely collaboratively with each other and with agencies across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Emergency Response and the Office of Faith-Based Partnerships worked together during heatwave alerts, and OME emailed heat warning and cooling center information to over 600,000 New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our Office of Faith-Based Partnerships tapped their stakeholder networks to get real-time updates of where New Yorkers were most impacted and used that information to recommend cooling center locations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: The Office of Faith-Based Partnerships and the Office of Community-Based Partnerships worked with the emergency response teams and MOIA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: to broaden City Hall's reach by translating urgent safety messaging into relevant languages,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: contributing to an 800-entry long list of stakeholders and faith institutions for email blasts, and overall increasing the reach of rapid response messaging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our campaigns, borough organizing, and events teams have worked with the Department of Transportation to increase bus rider participation and feedback in the city's bus action plan,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: and with the mayor's office to protect tenants to reach out to tenants living in distressed buildings throughout the city, as well as to landlords and property owners, enabling thousands of New Yorkers to participate in strengthening their communities and government.

chapters.summary: Van Auken introduces CEC Chair Dr. Sarah Saeed, noting 134,000 New Yorkers participated in participatory budgeting with 26,000 non-English ballots; Chief Service Officer Laura Rogg of NYC Service supporting 900,000 people; and Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz of the Public Engagement Unit.
chapters.title: Van Auken introduces Civic Engagement Commission, NYC Service, and PEU leaders

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: The OME umbrella also includes a few incredible offices whose leadership will be available for questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: The Civic Engagement Commission, and we have CEC Chair Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Sarah Saeed over here, which stewards participatory budgeting and language support at poll sites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Over 134,000 New Yorkers made their voice heard in the People's Money Participatory Budgeting Program in 2026, with over 26,000 ballots in a language other than English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: New York City Service, and we have Chief Service Officer Laura Rogg over here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: New York City service, which seeds a spirit of volunteerism across the city, bringing people together to support each other and our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Service envisions a city where New Yorkers are united by service, building a culture where neighbors uplift one another and take shared responsibility for the success of our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: This year, New York City Service has supported over 900,000 people through its service-based programs and partnerships with over 50,000 people engaged in service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: The Public Engagement Unit, and we have Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz right here, which connects New Yorkers to benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Their staff has highly skilled outreach specialists who knock on doors, make calls, send peer-to-peer texts, and much more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: For example, when the federal government passed new work requirements for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: putting thousands of people at risk of losing their benefits, PEU mobilized to inform SNAP recipients who were highest risk of losing their benefits as a result of the federal government policy changes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: By knocking on more than 10,000 doors and making more than 40,000 person-to-person phone calls, we reached 11,000 New Yorkers to help them keep their SNAP benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: OME's goal is to foster a spirit of civic engagement across the city, and we welcome opportunities to partner with the council and council members to better serve New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Van Auken says the city faces extreme weather, a cost of living crisis, deepening inequality, and all-time low trust in government, and that OME is scaling historic civic engagement traditions while forging new models to involve New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Van Auken concludes with challenges of extreme weather and eroding trust

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: New York City has a long history of wielding the power of our city government to engage New Yorkers borough by borough, neighborhood by neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: But today, we face new challenges and at a different scale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: More extreme weather, a cost of living crisis, and deepening inequality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Trust in government is at an all-time low, eroding our ability to get feedback and craft responsive policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: OME is both scaling up historic traditions of civic engagement and forging new models to get all New Yorkers involved in meeting today's challenges and building an affordable future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brewer notes Executive Order 23 gave the mayor's communications office authority over the Office of Ethnic and Community Media without rescinding Executive Order 7, and asks Van Auken to explain what happened to that office; Van Auken confirms it now lives under the communications team and refers further questions there.
chapters.title: Brewer asks Van Auken about Office of Ethnic and Community Media's move to communications

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We've been joined by Council Members Dinowitz and Morano and Felice on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I will call on my colleagues for questions in a minute.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just, I have a few.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Just to talk a little bit more about mass engagement and the structure.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know that you have public engagement, faith-based and community partnerships, New York City Service.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mentioned some of the other ones that you're welcome to include, but I'm interested in ethnic and community media, which I think is now under comms.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And can you just explain, there was an Executive Order 23 in September, recently,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: which gave the mayor's office of communications authority over that office, but it did not mention rescinding Executive Order 7.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, that's the office that has a lot of discussion.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Can you?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: explain what your office does and then what happened to this office if it's not part of you anymore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: The Office of Community and Ethnic Media does indeed live under the Mayor's Communication Team and not the Office of Mass Engagement, per the executive order you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I don't have many details, and I'm happy to get back to you, but I would refer you to the comms office for further details about the mayor's office of community and ethnic media.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I do know that they have a new executive director who will be starting soon.

chapters.summary: Brewer notes Mazin Minaham will head the Office of Ethnic and Community Media and asks about Amelia Rowland's role in that office; Van Auken says she must refer Brewer to the communications department for details.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about Amelia Rowland's role; Van Auken defers to communications

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Right, that's Mazin Minaham who will be head of the Office of Ethnic and Community Media, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But Amelia Rowland, she's now also in that office, and what's her role?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you know?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll have to refer you to the communications department for further details.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how a city employee is supposed to know what counts as substantive versus transitory, giving the example of sending out policy material; Smith-Cruz says determination is based on continuous training, liaison relationships, quarterly records management officer meetings, and onboarding.
chapters.title: Brewer presses Smith-Cruz on how employees determine what is substantive

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, and then also just for Adora, so I understand what you're stating in terms of substantive.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't know what that means, though.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, how is one supposed to know?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What gets included in what you would say should stay in the archival world.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How is one supposed to know that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because to me, sending out material regarding policy on, I don't know, composting, anything, would be substantive.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Chair, I would say that people know what's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Substantive is based on training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And we have lots of training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Training is continuous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It's both at Doris and at the agencies citywide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So the way that we administer training at Doris is we have multiple methods of sharing information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So I'm calling it training, but it's also information sharing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It includes a liaison model where there is a one-to-one relationship between liaisons at Doris and the agency's records management officer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: They can speak to each other anytime, and they're sort of on speed dial with each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We also have quarterly records management officer meetings for which Doris oversees, and all of the records management officers come.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: They receive updates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: They receive new policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: They're given guidance, and they're also given the opportunity for feedback and conversation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And ultimately, it's a professional development moment during those meetings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Finally, we have training as part of a new employee onboarding, including a presence on the DCAS's video learning platform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So that oversees, that overviews records management policies and principles for all employees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Most recently, we did supply guidance in April of 2026 to all agencies to support the determination and discernment of transitory versus substantive messages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And it was formatted as like a one pager, so to speak, like nicely designed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And it was an easy to follow summary guidance with recommended actions and practices to avoid, which linked to the platform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: policies and reiterated that instant messages and text messages are considered transitory and should not be used as the only record of substantive discussion policy or final decisions.

chapters.summary: Brewer gives the example of a message about a mayor's press conference on DoorDash and asks whether that would be substantive and require moving off Signal; Smith-Cruz says records management focuses on the function of the record and it is ultimately up to the agency and user to determine.
chapters.title: Brewer asks whether press conference material on Signal must be moved

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what, in other words, when somebody sends out material regarding some of the topics that I mentioned or getting out information today about a wonderful 11 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Press conference that the mayor's having about DoorDash and gain lots of money for the city and blah, blah, blah.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That would be substantive to me.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So that would mean that it would have to be, as I understand your guidance, would have to be taken off of Signal and put onto a different platform.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Or that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand what we're talking about today.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What does it fit into?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I would say the way to approach it is that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Records management focuses on the function of the record or the function that we operate in as business, as city business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so it's not focused on, say,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Let me say it differently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It's up to the agencies to determine what, to help support their staff in understanding what is substantive and transitory ultimately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So it's really up to the user.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: One should, in their utterance of the words, have a sense of whether something is transitory or not, or substantive or not, before they decide what platform it should exist in.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In my world of 40 years, that means it needs some help.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In terms of defining what it is.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether material sent via Signal would be subject to FOIL and therefore retained; Smith-Cruz explains FOIL only covers records city agencies possess or maintain, and instant messages are not considered records under the DORIS 2025 policy, so they are not required to exist.
chapters.title: Brewer asks whether Signal messages are FOILable and must be retained

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I would just say, but that's helpful that what you are stating.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In terms of foil, now, again, I'm a foil nut, just like I'm an archive nut.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So then the question is, all of this material is going out under signal or anything else.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Wouldn't that be foilable?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And if it's foilable, wouldn't it have to be?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: retained?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The Freedom of Information Law governs records, and that's what FOIL is in reference to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But under the Freedom of Information Law, it's only records that the city agencies possess or maintain that need to be produced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So as long as it exists,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: as a record within city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: If it's an active record, if it's a record that's archived, if it's a record that sits in its retention schedule, it's in a box in a warehouse, we can grab it and send it off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But if it does not exist, instant messages are not considered records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I think that's the issue that we're coming up against.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So they don't require attention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So they can exist, but they're not required to exist as records under the DORIS 2025 policy.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yeah, I think this one needs updating.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We're definitely open to talking with you about the policy as it stands.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how OME decides what campaigns to run and how it measures success; Van Auken says campaigns focus on issues New Yorkers raise like affordability, cites the current Talk to Tenants campaign with HPD and the mayor's office to protect tenants, and notes the Rent Guidelines Board turnout campaign doubled turnout.
chapters.title: Brewer asks Van Auken how OME decides on campaigns and measures success

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In terms of the Office of Mass Engagement, you listed some of the wonderful things that you're doing, and you did it in a very clear fashion because I didn't know what the hell the office did before that, so I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But can you just give us...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: some, like, just generally, are there, like, how many initiatives you're working on?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You mentioned some of them, but how do you decide what's going to be a campaign?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you decide what you're going to work on?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
