utterances.text: How does that process work?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our main focus with our campaigns is that they are touching on the issues that New Yorkers bring up time and time again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: So often that centers around affordability in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We are in month nine, so we are still in the beginning of this work, and we really look forward to working with you, other council members, on future campaigns that might be worthwhile.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We know that you all really understand your constituents and have your ears to the ground, and so we're very interested in collaborating.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Most of the time we're building campaigns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: So our current campaign is, just to give you an example, is called Talk to Tenants, and it's an outreach campaign to tenants who live in buildings with high rates of violation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: This campaign, we are not running it in a vacuum, so we are working on this outreach campaign along with the mayor's office to protect tenants and HPD's partners in preservation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: So our work is also defined by work that other agencies are doing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, how do you, I mean, I see.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I certainly went to the forum in East Harlem, but I saw all the follow-up that takes place, and then the next step is to do what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But how do you measure success for any campaign?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I suppose in your situation, you could see, do X number of buildings get the services they need, and are people not calling 311?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you measure success for a campaign?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I love that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We think a lot about that, and I think it really varies depending on what the purpose of the campaign is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: So our current campaign, Talk to Tenants, we want to make sure that tenants understand their rights and that they know how to connect to other tenants and they know how to form a tenant union and fight for their rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Earlier this year, we ran a shorter campaign to increase turnout at the Rent Guidelines Board hearings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: And as an example to your question, our goal there was to increase turnout to the hearings, which we did.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Turnout more than doubled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: So it really depends on what the campaign is about, what the outreach is about, and what we're hoping to help support New Yorkers in doing through the work.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The public advocate and I have testified at those damn hearings for the last hundred years, and so you definitely did turn out more people, I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That was good.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what the special projects unit does; Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz explains it is a field team focused on benefits access, conducting door-to-door, phone, and peer-to-peer text outreach to connect New Yorkers to SNAP, fair fares, and child care, and spearheaded SNAP work requirement outreach.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about the Public Engagement Unit's special projects team

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The special projects unit is part of the public engagement unit.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What does the special projects unit?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it over to Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: I appreciate the opportunity to be able to speak about the work we do at PEU.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: Our special projects team is one of the two main core programs of the public engagement unit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: This team primarily focuses on benefits access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: This is a field team dedicated to conduct outreach to connect New Yorkers to the benefits and services that they may be eligible for and that are available to them through the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: We conduct outreach door-to-door, via phones, via peer-to-peer text messages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: And focus on hand-holding New Yorkers in navigating the complexities of services like SNAP, fair fares, child care, and more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: More recently, this team spearheaded our outreach around the SNAP work eligibility requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: door-knocked more than 10,000 doors, made more than 40,000 phone calls, and spoke with over 11,000 New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: to inform them about the work eligibility requirements and make sure that the people understood the actions they needed to take in order to keep their benefits.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether PEU will publish outcomes of SNAP outreach and whether it uses influencers; De La Cruz says publishing falls under the Department of Social Services and that PEU does not work with influencers and has no budget for it.
chapters.title: Brewer asks De La Cruz about publishing SNAP outcomes and using influencers

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So that would be a situation where you could use influencers to tell

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: people that they need to sign up in order to not lose their benefits for work or volunteer.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have some sense of whether you've done that, number one?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And number two, are you going to be publishing for the public to know?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, I have been in enough forums and all the numbers, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: For those who would be cut off,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: if in fact they don't participate and volunteer or work, whatever other crazy ideas the federal government has.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So are you going to be telling the public what kinds of efforts have been successful, number one, and number two, do you use influencers to talk about what you're doing or to help you do what you do?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: To your question about whether we're going to be telling the public about how to make sure that they keep their benefits, we're going to continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you, will you be telling people what the outcome is?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, successful.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There's a huge number of New Yorkers who would be cut off if they do not participate, right?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So will you be publishing that information as to what's been successful or not?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: I think that falls under the scope of the Department of Social Services.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: To publish the information?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What about using influencers to get your message?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is that something that you're doing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: We do not work with influencers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: We do not have budget for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: I mean, our core priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: to make sure that as many New Yorkers as possible are aware about the benefits and services that they need, making sure that as many New Yorkers as possible know about changes that may come

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: to the benefits and services available to them through the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: We welcome the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deputy Commissioner De La Cruz
utterances.text: To work with people who are interested in spreading that message, but we do not work with influencers at this time.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what safeguards ensure OME does not engage in political work and what training exists; Van Auken says established legal rules govern separation of government and political activity and that everyone in the office takes them seriously, but she would follow up on training specifics.
chapters.title: Brewer asks Van Auken about safeguards against political work

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Back to the commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What safeguards are in place to ensure that the office is not engaging in political work?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: There are established legal rules governing separation between government activity and political activity, and our office, everyone in it, operates within those rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I take those rules very seriously, and everyone in our office takes those rules very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our office's work is focused on government functions, connecting New Yorkers to services and information, soliciting public opinion, and expanding participation in civic life.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, so what kind of training do you do to make sure that people don't do political work?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's hard sometimes for people not to do that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They don't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: It's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We do have different trainings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I would have to follow up with you on the specifics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I would be interested.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: But it's something that we take very seriously across the office.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about a January memo from the mayor's chief counsel telling mayoral agencies not to use Signal; Van Auken says OME does not use Signal and communicates via city email, phones, and Teams chats, while Brewer notes the memo went out to everyone.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about chief counsel memo banning Signal and OME's communication tools

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And now back to signals.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I understand that in January, the head of the chief counsel to the mayor.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Said to all mayoral agencies, do not use signal.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that memo?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Have you paid any attention to it?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Or that wouldn't be under you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That would be under the other office of communications.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If you guys don't use signal, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We do not use signal as an office.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how do you communicate with your many offices?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, you've got to...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All the people you're engaging with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: That's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We use our city email, our city phones, our city teams chats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So you know it's my understanding that that memo did go out to everybody, so it's kind of strange that we're all using Signal for communication.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We can use it for other things.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I will now call on Minority Leader Carr and then Public Advocate Williams to ask questions.

chapters.summary: Carr asks how many social media influencers have worked with the mayor's office or city agencies this calendar year; both Smith-Cruz and Van Auken say they do not have the answer and refer him to the communications department, with Brewer noting the communications office declined to participate.
chapters.title: Carr asks how many influencers worked with the mayor's office; panel defers

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you again, Chair Brewer, Commissioners.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Good to see you both.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you for being here today.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: My first question is, how many social media influencers have worked with the mayor's office or the various city agencies since the beginning of the calendar year?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Doris would not have the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We do not have the answer to that question either.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I would refer you to the communications department.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So we're having a hearing about this very topic, and two agency heads were sent here who don't have the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Just so you know, they were invited, and they declined to participate.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Just so you know, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I wonder why they declined.

chapters.summary: Carr asks how much the city has spent on social media influencer campaigns and how budgets are determined; Van Auken says she does not have that information, and Carr notes the panel was sent missing crucial components of the administration.
chapters.title: Carr asks about spending on influencer campaigns; Van Auken lacks information

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: How much has the city spent on the campaign so far, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: On these campaigns of social media influencers, do you know how much has been spent?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I do not have that information.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: No, okay.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I think we're going to get the same answer here, but I'm going to ask anyway.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Do you know what the costs are for each campaign and how those amounts and budgets are determined?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, but I do not have that answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Carr asks for examples of how influencer relationships with contracting agencies work and what public disclosure rules apply; Van Auken repeatedly refers him to the communications department, saying OME focuses on face-to-face communication.
chapters.title: Carr asks how influencer relationships are solicited and disclosed

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Can you provide an example of how the relationships work between the social media influencers and the contracting officer agency?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: How the relationship is solicited, how they're determined, who is chosen or approached to do those kinds of third-party communications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Our office is very focused on face-to-face communication, so for that question I would also refer you to the communications.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So again, a face-to-face agency or office is here speaking on behalf of the administration on a topic that has nothing to do with face-to-face communications.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: What are the rules for publicly disclosing?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: these kinds of relationships.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I would refer you to the comms department.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Where can the public find any information relating to this topic?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Who's collaborating with the various agencies and offices and the breakdown of who's being paid, who they are, et cetera, what kind of messaging they're doing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Again, I would refer you to the communications department.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Are there any requirements that these disclosures are a part of messages themselves?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I don't have any details about that.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Carr asks whether the mayor's office or agencies received guidance from the Conflicts of Interest Board or Law Department on disclosing influencer relationships and preserving records; Smith-Cruz says COIB has not submitted any guidance to DORIS, and Van Auken says she lacks details.
chapters.title: Carr asks about COIB or Law Department guidance on influencer disclosures

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Has the mayor's office or any agency saw guidance from COIB or the law department or any other entity on how to properly disclose any of these relationships to the public and what records should be preserved about communications with these influencers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I don't have those details.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I would refer you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And I could respond.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question related to records that would be retained.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Can you just ask that portion of the question again?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So has the mayor's office or any agency, including, I guess, Doris, saw guidance from the Conflicts of Interest Board or the law department or any other entity

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: on how to properly disclose any of these relationships with social media influencers to the public and what records relating to those relationships or those communications should be preserved?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I would say that the Conflicts of Interest Board has not submitted to us any guidance or any information related to this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: If it is created, then we would likely receive it at some point down the line when the records are transferred over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But we haven't received anything.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So nothing on the end of Doris, but you couldn't speak to the other parts of city government?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to speak to those parts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Carr says the questions that needed answering were not answered, criticizing that the panel was sent missing crucial components who could speak to who the influencers are, why they were contracted, and on what topics, and says oversight only works when both branches participate.
chapters.title: Carr criticizes administration's refusal to send communications officials

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: You know, I...

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I mean, obviously, the questions that I think really needed to be answered are not being answered here today.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And I think that the panel that was sent here was sent missing crucial components, crucial parts of the administration who could talk in more detail about the very topic of the hearing we're looking to address, which is...

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Who are the social media influencers that have been contracted either by the mayor's office or other parts of city government to do third party messaging?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: For what purpose?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: On what topics?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I think that these are crucial oversight issues that we're duly impaneled to address.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And I think the chair again for for bringing us together to try to get those answers.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: But oversight only works when.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Both sides of the divide between the legislature and the executive participate in the process.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So I appreciate all of you coming here to talk about your particular slices of this pie.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I think they're part of the conversation too, but it's incredibly disappointing and just outright ridiculous that we're having a hearing on a very important topic, a topic that was clearly defined

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And no one who is able to talk about the meat and potatoes of this issue from the perspective of the administration or the.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Mayor's office is here today to do so.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So with that being said, I turn it back to the chair.

chapters.summary: Williams says he agrees with Carr that the right people should be here, then asks whether messages through text, Signal, or WhatsApp do not have to be retained; Smith-Cruz confirms that under the policy instant messages are transitory with no expectation of retention, so deletion alone is not a violation.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Williams questions whether deleted messages break any law

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I really appreciate what you had to say, Public Advocate Williams, and then Councilmember Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As everyone knows, I have a great respect for this administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So it upsets me that they have me agreeing with Councilman McCarr very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But I am also disappointed that the communications of folks who should be here are not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I am coming from the point of view that I don't know that anything was wrong, done wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But there were questions that were raised by this article that I believe the public should hear answers to so that they can feel sure that nothing wrong occurred.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But the fact that the correct folks aren't here doesn't really help that story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so I don't know what to say except the right people should be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So that we can ask questions and people can hear the answers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so it is frustrating that that hasn't happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But I do want to ask some questions about what was testified.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I will say my belief is that most elected officials are struggling with this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So having a better understanding is really important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I just want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Is it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Is it the understanding of the law that messages through text, through signal, through WhatsApp do not have to be retained because of the nature of the communication?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Public Advocate Williams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The nature of how a record is structured and how we define records and the nature of using instant messaging, any type of instant messaging, is that it is transitory and so there is no expectation for their attention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I want to reclaim what that means, no expectation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So if it's not retained, there's no law or policy that's been broken.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: No, please say more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This is actually, I think, probably news to a lot of folks who are hearing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I think as we've struggled with this, retention has been more on the, leaning more on the retention side than not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I'm really interested in really fleshing this out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So you can feel free to say more.

chapters.summary: Director of Records Management Rose Nagel-Indigoyen explains records are scheduled by function rather than format, that instant messaging is intended for brief communications with zero retention by default, and that users must move substantive messages to preservable formats.
chapters.title: Rose Nagel-Indigoyen explains records are scheduled by function, not format

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I want to pass it over to the Director of Records Management, Riznagel Indigo.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Indigo Yen for some deep explanation here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: So thank you for the question, and thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: Records are scheduled according to their function, not according to the format in which they exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: And that is true for all records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: The format of instant messaging is intended for instant messages, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: Short communications that convey a brief message.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: The format does not provide the opportunity for preservation natively in these applications for the most part.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: So the policy of the city of New York, the 2025 policy, as our commissioner indicated, states that by default, these messages

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: that a person would choose to send in this format is considered to be transitory and has a zero retention period.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: If somebody finds that they have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: created a substantive message in this format.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: They are charged.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: with the responsibility of moving it to a format that allows for preservation and access.

chapters.summary: Williams asks whether the city must respond to FOIL requests for text messages; Smith-Cruz says FOIL only applies to records that exist, and if a text was deleted and no longer exists, the city cannot produce it, prompting Williams to note this is news to many.
chapters.title: Williams asks about FOIL requests for deleted texts; Smith-Cruz says no record exists

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Okay, so it's up to each one to determine whether or not they have sent a septic message.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rose Nagel-Indigoyen
utterances.text: That is what the policy states, yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So when Governor Cuomo switched to BlackBerry to try to get away from communication, he didn't have to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: He could have just stuck with Signal or WhatsApp.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I'm grabbing it back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about Governor Cuomo's BlackBerry use, but I will say that there is, we provide as a city many modes of communication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So we have, and the city oversees specific platforms, and we know what those are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: email, our SharePoint suite, Outlook, which is also email, OneDrive, there are various electronic records that we have access to and that we're able to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: adequately archive or retain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And those that don't exist on those platforms are unfortunately unable to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: they are not able to be retained, technologically speaking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So if we get four requests for texts, let's say regular text message, SMS, we don't have to respond in your view to those four requests for text messages?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: When you receive a FOIL request, if the record

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: exists, then one should go ahead and find the record.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So I think that whether or not we have access to those messages, those text messages, may be dependent upon the individual.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: If they are no longer here in government, if they're currently here, if the text

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: exists at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So if it's a record that exists, then...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But if it didn't because it was deleted, nothing wrong had happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We aren't able to provide FOIL responses to records that do not exist, correct?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Okay, this is quite interesting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm going to have probably some follow-up off, like I just want to have, this is very interesting to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We would love to talk to you more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'd love to talk to you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'd also love to talk to communications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so, again, I just want to reiterate, I think for New Yorkers and small and ethnic media that have been really trying to get access, they deserve to hear some of the answers to their questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So thank you, and thank you, Madam Chair.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how anyone would know whether a Signal message to influencers is substantive; Smith-Cruz cites DORIS's online list of over 100 records management definitions and the policy's definition of substantive messages as those documenting decisions, actions, or policies, and says DORIS does not monitor agency communications.
chapters.title: Brewer asks for the definition of substantive versus transitory messages

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Just back to this substantive picking up on the public advocate.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is there a review for whether something is substantive versus transitory?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm not sure I would know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, how do we know that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Example, you're sending something out signal via signal.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's to a group of influencers.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You get a response back from one that is a very substantive response.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It gets deleted under perhaps, perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But how would I know?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: if that was substantive or not?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What's the definition?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And in fact, Doris does create a list of definitions that exist for all agencies to see.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It's online for anybody to see.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We have over 100 definitions of records management terms and what they mean.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But the substantive messages definition was pulled out and put into the policy for the 2025 policy for instant messaging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And it states that it's on page two, right beneath transitory.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And it states substantive messages or messages which document or relate to the decisions, actions, or policies of a city office or agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And it identifies those messages as being those that ought to be, they must be retained and transferred to a format and platform that allows for their proper preservation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Doris does not monitor city agency communications, so I can't speak to any particular incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I never would be able to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But that said, the deletion of instant messages or text messages is not in and of itself a violation of the citywide policy, the 2025 citywide policy of Doris.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Next is Councilmember Wilson and then Councilmember Dinowitz.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks whether DORIS assesses if substantive government messages were deleted before preservation for agencies using Signal; Smith-Cruz says DORIS does not monitor active communication channels and anticipates agencies received needed training to make those determinations themselves.
chapters.title: Council Member Wilson asks whether DORIS assesses deleted substantive messages

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So in relation to the signal activity, that's the topic of this hearing today, has Doris assessed whether substantive government messages were deleted before they could be preserved?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How do you assess that?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: for any agency that may engage in signal activity?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Doris does not monitor active communication channels within government employees, so we're not able to do that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But we do anticipate that each agency has received the training that they need to make those delineations on their own.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So there's, if the, if a user, if the impetus is on the user to decide whether a message is transitory or substantive, there is, there is training provided to those agencies so that their

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: staff can make that decision?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks whether there is a preferred internal communication platform; Smith-Cruz says the 2025 policy does not distinguish internal from external instant messaging, DORIS provides guidance on platforms but Signal is not written into any policy, and social media policy was last updated in 2021.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about preferred communication platforms and Signal's status

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I'll say a little bit more about it since we're asking continually.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And I think, oh, Williams left.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I was going to quote him, but I won't quote him now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: To say that though we do not typically create specific guidance related to formats, the policy on instant messaging was created and generated in consultation with the law department and the office of the chief counsel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so we don't limit any authority to any use of specific platforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We just provide guidance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And, of course, city agencies may be the ones to provide stricter policies related to specific.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: specific platforms because of the training that we provide with them, provide to them and the guidance we provide to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So nothing in the current policy prohibits the use of signal messaging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And we sort of set it as a floor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And not the ceiling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So we say this is the bare minimum of what you need to know, and then agencies may take it upon themselves to provide additional guidance, and that's how we would anticipate their communication around what they should or should not be using for specific conversations.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Regarding internal communications in agencies, is there a specific preference in terms of what communication platforms are used?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: i.e.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Specific apps or messaging platforms?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Under the current 2025 instant messaging policy, there's no difference between internal and external for instant messaging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But as it relates to platforms as a whole, we do provide guidance on which platforms are best used for specific types of business.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Is Signal one of those?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We do not have signal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We don't have signal written actually in any policy, maybe because the policies were in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So, or that the latest update was in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Our social media policy was updated in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I don't know if signal was around then.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So mostly I would say that we do a lot of work to keep up to date with current practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And we acknowledge that the work of digital archiving has to move with how technology is shifting over time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And we are doing lots of work to get to that.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks how often the social media policy is reviewed; Smith-Cruz says it was last updated in 2021 with a Department of Investigation request at that time, and Wilson suggests regularly occurring reviews given how quickly technology moves, which Smith-Cruz welcomes.
chapters.title: Wilson suggests regular review of social media policy; Smith-Cruz welcomes feedback

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How often do you conduct a review of the social media policy?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The social media policy was last updated in 2021, and I unfortunately don't have any understanding of when it was initiated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I know there was a Department of Investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Requests during that time for when it was evaluated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I'm not sure what prompted that or what came to that point, but we led to this

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: policy that essentially puts social media at a place of permanence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so everything that is put to social media is permanently retained, which means that we keep it forever.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Given how quickly tech seems to be moving these days, it might make sense to have a regularly occurring review of these social media apps and how they affect our government communication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that feedback.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Councilmember Dindowitz and then Councilmember Wong.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz reads the DORIS definition of substantive messages and asks whether daily updates, talking points, and clips shared via Signal would be substantive; Smith-Cruz says records management is based on function not format and that communications about records are transitory, frustrating Dinowitz.
chapters.title: Council Member Dinowitz presses Smith-Cruz on whether talking points are substantive

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I also do want to associate myself with the remarks of both the public advocate and the minority leader that it is, I mean, disappointing at best that

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: the comms team who was invited is not in attendance, especially from a

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: administration that is supposed to be defined by transparency.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But I do want to ask about the instant messages.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You were discussing them as by nature transitory, brief messages.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm reading something from Doris, and I just want to make sure I'm reading this correctly from 2024.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It says instant electronic messages, and it defines

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: substantive messages which document or relate to the decisions, actions, or policies of a city office or agency, and then it defines transitory messages which do not document or relate to the decisions, actions, or policies of an agency,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: such as personal messages between coworkers and time-dependent communications,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: purely logistical, such as arranging a time or place for a meeting or call.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's correct?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's still correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It may be that you're citing the instant messaging policy of 2024 and there was a 2025 update, but the language is similar to the current 2025 update.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, so you had said in the, or I think you had said in the testimony,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: about a brief message is for the nature of instant messages.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And then according to the Columbia report, which first documented, it says via the encrypted messaging app signal, messages receive, members receive daily updates, talking points, and clips to use in their points.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Would you consider those to be

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: brief or transitory messages, or would you consider those to be substantive messages?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I would say that Doris is not charged with monitoring.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm asking what you think.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You've created a policy.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to monitor it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm asking your opinion based on documents that you produce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So the way that records management works is that it's based on the function and it's not based on the format.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so we really want to identify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the format.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm asking about what's in the message.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Would Doris consider daily updates, talking points, and clips to use in posts?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: substantive, which documents or relate

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: to decisions, actions, or policies of a city officer or agency, or would you consider that to be personal messages between coworkers, time-dependent communication regarding purely logistical matters?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification of your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I would say that we see those

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: points that you're, and you could list a whole list of things, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I could give you a calendar, I could give you, you know, press releases, all the things, and ultimately these would be duplicative to the actual object.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so what we retain are the records themselves, and the communications about records are what would be transitory.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks whether all text messages are transitory and whether sending links to documents stored on OneDrive would avoid FOIL; Smith-Cruz says DORIS would never advise avoiding FOIL, that the record is the document not the link, and that agencies should consider how employees use instant messaging.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks if linking to OneDrive documents makes messages transitory

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can you say that in English, please?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So an example is if you create, thank you for that humor, if you create a document and you save it on your hard drive, or I don't know what we save things on, you save it in your OneDrive, and that's where it lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And that would be the record, the document itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But if you have drafts of the document, if you have specific, I don't know, like there's moments where you're communicating between folks, but there is a physical object and you want to say you'd send a link.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Here's a link to the document that I just wrote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So the link can be something that leads to the actual record, which is the document.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The record is the document, not the link.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So the actual, so it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So in essence.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All text messages are transitory.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So your recommendation for me, if I don't ever want to be foiled, is to put everything on my OneDrive and just send my communications with links over instant messaging because by definition they would then be transitory.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I would never advise you to not want to be foiled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We're here for transparency, and that's really important, and we believe in that in our work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But I would say that we recommend that agencies take the responsibility of considering how they would like their employees to use instant messaging if they're going to use instant messaging at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But I want to understand that if...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And to provide guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, your guidance is.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But if a message has...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Daily updates, talking points, and clips to use in post.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm just quoting an article here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I would read it as that's a substantive message.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It has documents that relate to decisions, actions, or policies in the officer agency.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But what I'm hearing you say is not really, because if you just include a link,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It doesn't really count.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's kind of what I'm hearing the official guidance to be from Doris.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says the official DORIS guidance discourages substantive instant messages and it seems the team doing these messages did not do their job properly, then thanks the panel and turns it back to the chair.
chapters.title: Dinowitz concludes the mayor's messaging team did not follow DORIS policy

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And I will say the official guidance from Doris is in the policy, and the guidance does state it bold and underline that employers are strongly discouraged from creating electronic messages that are substantive in nature,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: and that it is the responsibility of the agency to understand what substantive messages are.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, I understand the amount of time, but it seems like...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like the team that was doing these instant messages didn't do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's how it seems based on your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I'll turn it back to the chair, but I want to thank you all for coming and testifying today and for your answers to the questions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Wong and then Councilmember Morano.

chapters.summary: Wong notes the room is packed with only three empty seats, cites the charter giving committees authority to require testimony, and asks where Amelia Rowland, the Director of New Media overseeing the influencer operation, is; Van Auken says she does not have the answer.
chapters.title: Council Member Wong notes packed room and asks where Amelia Rowland is

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And thank you to Speaker Menon for the opportunity to hold this hearing on this important issue and the bills before the committee today.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Now, I counted, there are only like three empty seats in the room.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: There are 64 seats in the room.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So this is a packed room.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So the people here, they are here today because this issue is important.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And I'm glad the panelists are here because this is an important topic.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And the charter expressly gives council committees the authority to require the attendance and testimony of the people necessary to an inquiry.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And we're asking about today, very importantly, signal.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Signal and the person.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Amelia Rowland, the Director of New Media and Cultural Communications, appears to have all the answers, but she's not here.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So I have to ask the obvious, where is Amelia Rowland today?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Does the panel know?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Anybody know where she is?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I do not have the answer to that question right now.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, and she has been publicly identified as the official overseeing the influencer operation and the signal group at the center of today's hearing.

chapters.summary: Wong asks if DORIS plans to archive Signal; Smith-Cruz says if it were true it would be through the third-party social media archiving platform, but currently there is no technological possibility to archive Signal, and instant messaging behavior is not retained regardless of platform.
chapters.title: Wong asks Smith-Cruz whether DORIS plans to archive Signal

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my first question to the Commissioner of Doris.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Do you plan to archive signal?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Commissioner Wong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I mean, I'm sorry, Commissioner Wong, Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I would say that if it were true that we were planning to archive Signal, it would be through the third-party platform that we use to archive social media.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And if there is the possibility, and if they were to adopt that platform, then it would fall into alignment with the other platforms that we do archive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But currently, there is no technological possibility to archive Signal as a platform, as a software.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And the current policy for instant messaging does acknowledge that if it's instant messaging behavior, regardless of platform, then we wouldn't retain those records within the archive specifically.

chapters.summary: Wong says a January 15 memo from Chief Counsel Ramsey Kassem bans Signal for all city employees and asks why the mayor's office is using it; Smith-Cruz says she is not aware of the memo but that agencies ought to comply with DORIS policy and their own leadership's guidance.
chapters.title: Wong cites January memo banning Signal and asks why mayor's office uses it

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I have seen the memo.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: There's data in January that's issued to all city employees that signal is banned.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: No one could use it.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Are you aware of this memo?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a memo for banning signal, but I do know that there are very many agency communications related to guidance for what folks should use when they are.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It's dated January 15 from Chief Counsel Ramsey Kassem, and it specifically says do not use signal.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So why are we seeing the mayor's office using it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The best that I can say is that city agencies ought to comply with the DORIS policy and that additional guidance from their own

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: leadership ought to be something that they regard in their communications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But we do let everyone know, we provide access to the same policy to all city agencies, the same 2025 instant messaging policy.

chapters.summary: Wong asks who the committee should ask about the creation and management of the Signal group if Rowland and the chief counsel will not appear; Smith-Cruz says she is not sure but suggests the contact at Intergovernmental Affairs could help find someone who can answer.
chapters.title: Wong asks who can answer questions about the Signal group; Smith-Cruz suggests IGA

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: With Roland not here, and who exactly are we supposed to ask?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'm at this question for the panel.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Who exactly are we supposed to ask about the creation, operation, and management of the signal group in question?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: If the person identified is running it, nor the chief counsel who has direct oversight over these matters will not appear before the committee.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Where can we get answers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure, but I would say potentially your contact at Intergovernmental Affairs could support getting you to someone who can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It's unfortunate that we have a packed room and the person that has answers to the room is not here.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'll save my next set of questions for round two, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Councilmember Murano.

chapters.summary: Morano submits a three-page memorandum from the Mayor's Office of the Chief Counsel titled 'Communication Requirements and Best Practices,' dated January 15 with metadata suggesting 2026, which states employees should not use WhatsApp, Signal, or other communications apps for work, addressing document preservation, FOIL, and cybersecurity.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano enters chief counsel memo banning WhatsApp and Signal

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Chair Brewer and my colleague, Councilmember Wong, alluded to this, but I received this three-page memorandum, which I've asked the Sergeant at Arms to share with you, from the Mayor's Office of the Chief Counsel.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It's dated January 15, 2022, but it's a typo from what I understand, and the metadata suggests it's from January of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The memorandum is titled Communication Requirements and Best Practices.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: On page three, it states, and I quote, you should not use WhatsApp, Signal, or any other communications app or platform for work.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: This wasn't a casual suggestion.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The memo specifically addresses document preservation, FOIL compliance, and cybersecurity.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I've asked that this document be entered into the record, and I want to ask a couple of questions about it.

chapters.summary: Morano asks Smith-Cruz to confirm the memo's issuance; she says she was not around and DORIS does not fall within the chief counsel's jurisdiction, and confirms DORIS has not reviewed the influencer Signal group to determine whether substantive records were deleted.
chapters.title: Morano asks Smith-Cruz to confirm the memo and whether DORIS reviewed the Signal group

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Can you confirm, as best you understand, that this memorandum was issued by the Office of the Chief Counsel in January of 2026?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Councilmember Murano.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I can confirm that what you put in front of me is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: If it is, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I wasn't around during that time, and Doris would not receive memos to their staff because we don't fall within their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So it seems like this would be a memo.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: To the specific mayor's office employees, and we're not a part of that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So let me try to be more Doris-focused.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony, Commissioner, says that substantive messages must be transferred to another format for preservation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So under Doris's policy, messages documenting or relating to government decisions, actions, or policies have to be retained.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the influencer signal group to determine whether any substantive government records were deleted?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And the answer is we don't monitor communications for our current government employees.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Has anyone in city government conducted that review?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I wouldn't know if it were to happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It wouldn't happen from the Doris end.

chapters.summary: Morano asks who is responsible for determining whether records were lost and when that determination will be completed; Smith-Cruz says agencies are responsible for developing policies but retention of Signal instant messages is not within current records management policy.
chapters.title: Morano asks who is responsible for determining whether records were lost

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So who's responsible, again, not to repeat what my two colleagues were saying, but who specifically is responsible for determining whether records were lost and when will that determination be completed?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I would say in relation to the 2025 policy on instant messaging, it is the responsibility of agencies to develop and disseminate policies related to use of these materials.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: However, the retention of these materials, specifically signal instant messaging, is not within policy for records management.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Practice in the city currently.

chapters.summary: Morano notes RecordPoint manages 215 million records across 31 agencies including the mayor's office but only maps government-supplied tools, and asks if it captures Signal; Smith-Cruz confirms it cannot retain Signal and DORIS is not looking for it to since instant messaging has zero retention.
chapters.title: Morano asks whether RecordPoint captures Signal messages; Smith-Cruz says no

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner, page two of your testimony says that the city's record point system manages more than 215 million records across 31 agencies, including the mayor's office.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But you also say it only maps to government-supplied tools.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does that system automatically capture messages sent through Signal?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The RecordPoint electronic records management tool is robust, and it is able to coordinate alongside the categorization of records, and those categorizations are records that are managed through city government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: That we are vendors, that are vendors for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So the answer is that it would not be able to retain signal, and we aren't looking for it to because, again, the instant messaging does not sit within a retention schedule of more than zero.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether DORIS has any independent way to determine if an employee failed to transfer a substantive Signal message; Smith-Cruz says it is up to the individual user to transfer substantive messages and DORIS cannot do this, so compliance depends on individual employees recognizing what must be preserved.
chapters.title: Morano asks if DORIS can detect failure to transfer substantive messages

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does Doris have any independent way to determine whether an employee has failed to train?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Transfer a substantive signal message into an approved record system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You didn't say thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I do actually appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Ooh, that was a good one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And that you said substantive signal messages, and I don't believe that I know that that, if a message is substantive, then it is up to the agent.
