utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The user, the person who's writing the message, or receiving it for that matter, to transfer it to a different location.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It isn't a Doris process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It would be not possible for us to do this.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So is compliance effectively dependent on individual employees recognizing which messages must be preserved and transferring them themselves?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: To be compliant with the 2025 instant messaging policy, a user ought to participate in the process of transferring instant messages that are substantive if they exist.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I do hope because there are so many folks that could be answering these questions that aren't here that this committee and this council will consider using our subpoena power to force them to answer these questions,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: irrespective of whether we get a thank you for the question when those questions are proffered.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Morano says he hopes the committee will consider using subpoena power to force answers from those absent; Brewer agrees the committee is not getting the answers the hearing was outlined for and says the mayor's communications office should be there.
chapters.title: Morano suggests subpoena power; Brewer agrees communications office should appear

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I totally agree that we're not getting the answers that this hearing was outlined for, but we sure are.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: those at communications of the man's office to be here.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether Amelia Rowland or others got permission from DORIS to use Signal's auto-delete feature, noting city employees may not delete records without prior approval; Smith-Cruz says the approval requirement she references came from within a specific agency and is not part of DORIS policy, and agencies may impose stricter rules.
chapters.title: Brewer asks whether Rowland got approval for Signal's auto-delete feature

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have a question, and then I'll call on Council Member Wong for further second round.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So under the DARS rules, if we're trying to stay in the DARS rules, a city employee, as I understand it, needs to get approval to use the auto-delete feature on messaging apps.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Now, you could say, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If the signal communication was deleted.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We don't know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But it is an auto-delete feature, signal is.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, if that is the rule, number one, and second, did Amelia Rowland or anybody else who was doing communication with signal

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: get permission from Doris to use this auto-delete feature on the Signal app, or did they just get permission to use Signal in general?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because it seems to me that a city employee may not delete records without prior approval under Doris rules, which is slightly different than what you're stating.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Can you clarify this?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The request for approval that you're referencing, I believe, came through a communication within a specific agency and is not actually within the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Doris policy creation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: At the very minimum, city agencies need to, they're required to comply with the DORIS policy, but then, of course,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Core city agencies may impose stricter policies within themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So with respect to instant messaging platform, if that was a position within the agency, then I can't really speak to what they've chosen to determine there

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: because we don't have that within the instant messaging policy as it stands, a need for approval.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So there is no need for approval, is what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The need for approval may exist within an agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But not from Doris.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But not from Doris, correct.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, but we don't know if agencies have an approval process.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We don't know that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It would be up to the agency to have one or not have one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: If there is an approval process, I wouldn't know what their strategies are and how they communicate that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There's a lot of new legislation to be needed in all of this, I think is what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Without saying it, because you can't say it, but I can say it.

chapters.summary: Ariola says there is a fine line between agencies providing legitimate public information and using taxpayer dollars to promote political propaganda, that government communications should be factual and transparent, and that from what she hears there is little accountability over what is disseminated through outreach organizing.
chapters.title: Council Member Ariola warns against taxpayer-funded political propaganda

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right, because I was under the impression that Doris was given the approval.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Anyway, Councilmember Areola is on the Zoom and has a question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We do have a quorum, so she can ask it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Councilmember Areola?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so very much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So all the questions that have been asked have been exactly what was in line with the questions I was going to ask.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So I just want to say that there is a fine line between government agencies providing public and legitimate information and using taxpayer dollars to promote political propaganda.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Taxpayer-funded agencies have a responsibility to educate, inform, and provide essential services and not to use the public resources to advance a political agenda, influence public opinion, or promote a particular ideology.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Government communications should be factual, transparent, and directly connected to the agency's legitimate public purpose.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: There should be someone overseeing this.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: There is a line that is crossed when the issue is bigger than politics.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It becomes a question of accountability.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And from what I'm hearing today, there isn't very much accountability as to what is being disseminated through your outreach organizing.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You're using public dollars.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: They belong to the public.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: They should be used to serve the public and not promote political narratives.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I really do appreciate the time.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Councilmember Wong and then Councilmember Morano.

chapters.summary: Wong asks how DORIS handles encrypted messages on Signal and other platforms and what happens with auto-deletion; Smith-Cruz says DORIS does not access encrypted messages, which is why the retention schedule is zero, and distinguishes instant messaging from social media publications that are archived permanently.
chapters.title: Wong asks how DORIS handles encrypted messages and auto-deletion

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My first question is back to Commissioner Sean Smith-Cruz of Department of Records.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: As I understand that we have encrypted messages here, and it seemed to me that

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: There's no purpose of archiving them if you cannot read them.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So how do you handle encrypted messages?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And what's your policy?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because why are we archiving messages that we cannot read?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Where are you finding?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Can I just?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Signal.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Well, let's start with signal.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Oh, signal.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or other.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: There are other social media platforms that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: That support encryption.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my question is, how do you access these messages if they're encrypted?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We do not access the messages, which is why there is a retention schedule of zero.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So there is no expectation to archive signal currently.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And what about, what,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What about auto-deletion?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like other social media platforms support that too.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So what do you say about those records?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You cannot archive them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So if it's a social media platform, then the assumption there and the way that we're distinguishing between instant messaging and social media, which is why we have the two separate policies, is that social media is meant to be, is considered a publication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It's a thing that is posted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It is put out into the world already.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So a government official or an agent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: is publishing their works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It's like a YouTube video or an Instagram post.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: If the software posts it, then it is published.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so the software is able to be captured and retained as a result of that process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So it's technologically possible to do that for those types of platforms.

chapters.summary: Wong asks whether DORIS introduces corrective or recovery steps when records are destroyed without authorization and how the public accesses archived content; Smith-Cruz says social media captured at creation is preserved even if deleted later, and the public can access Archive Social, encouraging council members to connect their accounts.
chapters.title: Wong asks about recovery steps for destroyed records and public access

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But are you...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Are you introducing corrective and recovery steps when these records may have been destroyed or deleted without authorization?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: In the social media platform, if it has been captured on its point of creation, then it actually doesn't matter if it's deleted in its current state because it will have already been captured within the archiving social platform or software.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, because as I see it, if tax dollars are being paid for these social media platforms and they're exchanging messages as involving official business, it is your job to retain them and make the messages accessible to the public.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Continue to distinguish between the instant messaging feature of some of these softwares and platforms and the sort of publication feature of these softwares and platforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The instant messaging is transitory and is not being archived or retained.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And the publication feature is being archived in permanence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so we're keeping it forever.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And how would the public access them, like today, right now?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: If the public would like to, they could go to Archive Social and they could see what has been published across the various agencies around New York City, including City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We really do encourage you to make sure that your social media is connected to Archive Social and Simit Plus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And if you're not sure how to do that, you can contact the municipal library to get connected.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Wong asks whether OME maintains creator lists, communicates with influencers, or recommends creators to agencies; Van Auken says OME does not maintain creator lists, has coordinated with the communications team on occasion, and has not issued citywide standards for creator-based engagements.
chapters.title: Wong asks Van Auken whether OME maintains creator lists or standards

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: A question to Commissioner Van Alken, Office of Mass Engagement.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: On use of creators, does the OME or any office or program under its umbrella maintain the creator lists or communicate with influencers or recommend creators?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: To agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, our primary work at OME is to talk to New Yorkers face-to-face through all the different avenues of work that we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: On occasion, we have worked with the communications team to make sure that information about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: hearings or rights or services are being communicated to New Yorkers in as many ways as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: It's very important to this administration that we are reaching New Yorkers in many different ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: But I

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: I would have to refer you to the comms team for specifics.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Does OME maintain creator lists, communicate with influencers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: OME does not maintain creator lists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We have worked, we have coordinated with the comms team to work with creators on occasions, but you would have to refer to the comms team for details beyond that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Has the OME issued any citywide standards for creator-based engagements?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so, but we can get back to you with details.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Councilmember Morano.

chapters.summary: Morano asks what additional safeguards DORIS would need to ensure substantive government communications are preserved; Smith-Cruz says council advocacy helps, encourages agencies to document exceptions, and notes RecordPoint only covers government-supported software while social media archiving is handled by a vendor.
chapters.title: Morano asks what additional safeguards DORIS needs to preserve communications

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner, your testimony describes record management policies, employee training, and technological systems.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We also have a written policy telling employees not to use Signal, which we alluded to earlier, followed by an acknowledged incident involving disappearing messages.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What additional safeguards, if any?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Would Doris need to ensure substantive government communications are preserved, whether it's legislation, whether it's policy guidance?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What else would you need?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: We definitely enjoy these points of advocacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: that come up from city council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: It's very helpful to maintaining our request for agencies to communicate with their employees related to what they should be doing for their records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: So truly it's broadening understanding and ensuring that you two are

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: preserving your own records and submitting it to its proper channels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I know that the City Council, for example, has its archives at the LaGuardia Archives, which we were able to visit and get a tour of, and they have a new director.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And we've talked to them about the Memorandum of Understanding related to City Council and Doris's archival records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: The best way we can support the work of archiving the city is to have a sense of how our own records are being archived and maintained and hopping on board to the records management platform that allows us to do this work.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Would a requirement that agencies document exceptions and verify preservation settings address a gap in the current system, or can you already require that under existing authority?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And just to clarify, a requirement to verify, can you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: A requirement that agencies document exceptions and verify preservation settings in, say, a WhatsApp group, or I don't know how Signal works, but presumably there's something similar in Signal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you for that distinction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: As it relates to, thank you for the question as well, as it relates to the social media platforms, that is not what RecordPoint is capturing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so we set the parameters for the records management platform that we are supporting agencies to onboard into.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And that is for government-supported software.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: As it relates to the social media, then, the vendor is the one setting up the ability to scrape those platforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so it really is not, it's a very easy and foolproof method.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: They just.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Connect their account and they're already being archived if they have a social media archive social account.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Unfortunately, as of now, there really is no way for us to capture what takes place in specific platforms because the technology just doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: And so in some future moment, maybe it will exist and we'll continue to advance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: But as of now, the policy is set because of the limitation of technology as well as the likelihood that these messages are transitory and not really worth the government resources to retain in perpetuity the way that other materials eligible.

chapters.summary: Morano asks for a borough-by-borough breakdown of OME outreach spending, staffing, events, and service referrals, particularly for Staten Island; Van Auken notes a Staten Island community liaison and First Deputy Commissioner Singh describes flood and hurricane outreach and representation at the Postcards Memorial.
chapters.title: Morano asks Van Auken for borough-by-borough outreach breakdown, especially Staten Island

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And for Commissioner Van Alken, your office and the Office of Mass Engagement is supposed to bring government closer to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Can you provide a borough-by-borough breakdown of your outreach spending, staffing, community events, and completed service referrals?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In particular, I'm interested in what percentage has been directed to Staten Island and how are you measuring whether residents are actually receiving help?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Staten Island usually gets the short end of the stick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: We have a Staten Island community liaison.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tascha Van Auken
utterances.text: Some of the specifics I can't speak to you now and I can get back to you, but I want to pass it over to First Deputy Commissioner Singh to talk about some of the work we've done across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - First Deputy Commissioner Singh
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - First Deputy Commissioner Singh
utterances.text: As the Commissioner had stated, we take our responsibility to outreach and engage with all New Yorkers, no matter which borough they are in, very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - First Deputy Commissioner Singh
utterances.text: We have a Staten Island District Manager who is often on the island ensuring they are reaching out to various community-based organizations, faith-based organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - First Deputy Commissioner Singh
utterances.text: Just recently, they worked with our emergency response and recovery team around flooding and hurricane outreach to ensure that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - First Deputy Commissioner Singh
utterances.text: many of the faith and community organizations were aware of the flood zones that they live in and what are the options and availabilities available to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - First Deputy Commissioner Singh
utterances.text: They represented our office at the recent postcards memorial as well, which we make sure as an office we are turning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - First Deputy Commissioner Singh
utterances.text: And we continue to do great work on the borough.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yeah, if you could get me the borough-by-borough breakdown of spending, staffing, et cetera, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And hopefully I'll see the liaison at tonight's community board meeting.

chapters.summary: Amanda Melillo, First Deputy Executive Director of the CFB, describes the agency's nonpartisan mission, matching funds program, and NYC Votes initiative, which partners with social media influencers to share voting PSAs, bringing influencer selection in-house in 2023.
chapters.title: CFB's Amanda Melillo describes agency mission and NYC Votes influencer program

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Brewer and members of the Committee on Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: I am Amanda Molillo, First Deputy Executive Director of the New York City Campaign Finance Board.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: The CFB is a nonpartisan, independent city agency committed to strengthening our local democracy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: We combat the influence of big money in politics by amplifying the power of small dollar contributions from everyday New Yorkers through our matching funds program, which serves as a model nationwide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Through our NYC Votes initiative, we engage directly with voters and provide access to the information and resources they need to vote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: One way we do this is by partnering with social media influencers to share public service announcements about voting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: This approach is especially effective at reaching people who aren't normally tuned into government and politics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: In 2021, the CFB began working with influencers through our advertising vendor at the time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: And in 2023, we brought the work of identifying, researching, and selecting influencers in-house to our social media team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Over this time, we have built a trusted messenger program that partners with voices who can reach younger voters in ways traditional government outreach often does not.

chapters.summary: Melillo says the CFB prioritizes younger voters, non-English speakers, voters with disabilities, and those impacted by the criminal legal system in the South Bronx, South Brooklyn, and Queens, requires influencers to be NYC residents with majority local audiences, and includes nonpartisanship clauses barring candidate endorsements.
chapters.title: Melillo details influencer selection criteria and nonpartisanship safeguards

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: This strategic engagement is driven by our city charter mandate to prioritize communities, both demographic and geographic, that are underrepresented in the electoral process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: These priority audiences include younger voters under age 30, voters who primarily speak a language other than English,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: voters with disabilities, and voters who have been impacted by the criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: We also focus outreach on neighborhoods in the South Bronx, South Brooklyn, Northern Queens, and Central Queens that have lower voter turnout and a higher concentration of these priority audiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Our work with influencers reflects the CFB's broader commitment to reaching and engaging these audiences and communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: We take our position as a nonpartisan agency seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: The CFB uses clear criteria to select influencers based on their audience,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Each must be a New York City resident with a majority audience in the five boroughs, and we prioritize influencers who can reach our priority audiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Our internal nonpartisanship policy requires that all contracts include a nonpartisanship clause and an agreement not to endorse or oppose candidates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Starting from the date they begin working with the CFB until 90 days after the general election.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: These guardrails enable the agency to avoid working with influencers who have expressed opinions on candidates or taken positions on political parties, ballot proposals, or contentious partisan issues.

chapters.summary: Melillo says the CFB worked with 29 influencers generating over 70 posts on Instagram and TikTok at a total cost of $626,365, producing over 6 million views and 500,000 engagements with a 5% engagement rate, and that non-English content outperformed English posts.
chapters.title: Melillo reports 2025 influencer campaign results and costs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: In 2025, the CFB worked with 29 influencers over the election cycle who generated over 70 posts across Instagram and TikTok at a total cost of $626,365.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Compensation varies based on the campaign's strategic priority, the influencer's audience size and reach, and production complexity and creativity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: These posts produce more than 6 million views and over 500,000 engagements, with an average engagement rate of about 5%, well above the 1% to 3% industry average.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Every like, comment, and share signals a viewer engaging with a civic message and amplifies that content to be more visible to others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: The effect was even stronger for non-English content.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Influencer videos in Spanish, Mandarin, Korean, and Bengali created in language by voices based in the communities we aim to reach outperformed English language posts,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: generating over 2.3 million views and more than 4,000 visits to our NYC Votes website.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: These are audiences that have historically lacked civic engagement and election messaging in their own language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Our ability to engage

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: through trusted messenger influencers in language allows us to get them the information they need to be informed voters.

chapters.summary: Melillo notes the CFB had one week to review the four bills and says T2026-2553 by Council Member Wong duplicates existing CFB disclaimer rules, T2026-2555 by Carr broadens existing blackout law with no formal position, and T2026-1440 by Carr would disperse reporting obligations to individual public servants rather than agencies.
chapters.title: Melillo gives preliminary CFB feedback on the four bills

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Turning to the bills before the committee today, I want to note that the CFB has had one week to review the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: proposed four pieces of legislation, so our feedback at this stage is preliminary, and we look forward to providing more detailed comments and suggested edits to the council after conducting a more detailed analysis of the impact on CFB operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: However, from initial review, several of these bills raise serious concerns and as currently drafted would have unintended negative consequences for the agency's work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: The first bill I will discuss is T2026-2553 introduced by Councilmember Wong, which would codify paid-for-by disclaimer requirements on online and digital campaign expenditures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: CFB Rule 6-06 has required these disclaimers on all campaign advertising since the 2017 election cycle and was expanded in 2024 to cover additional communication types, including paid influencer content.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Such expenditures are already disclosed and documented like any other campaign advertising spending.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Rule 14-04 similarly requires disclaimers, uncovered communications by independent spenders, and visual, video, or audio formats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: This legislation appears to duplicate the existing disclaimer requirements without changing the current obligations of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: campaigns and we don't believe these changes are necessary to the charter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: T2026-2555 introduced by Councilmember Carr would prohibit candidates for office from appearing in certain digital or online government funded public communication during the 90 days preceding an election.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: The CFB already enforces the existing part of this law, which prohibits using governmental resources for mass mailings during this period.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: This bill would simply broaden the scope of communication types required under this law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: We have no substantive feedback at this time and have no formal position on this bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: T-2026-1440, sponsored by Councilmember Carr, would require public servants to report spending on public communications paid for with government resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: As drafted, the reporting obligation falls on the individual public servant who authorizes the use of government funds, which could unnecessarily disperse responsibilities across an agency and lead to duplicative or missed reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: We believe agency-level reporting through existing advertising spending reporting would better achieve this goal while consolidating reporting obligations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Given these concerns, the CFB does not support the bills currently drafted, but we welcome further discussion with the Council to share our perspectives as an agency that funds public communications.

chapters.summary: Melillo says T2026-2554 by Council Member Feliz raises fundamental concerns because designating the CFB as an enforcing agency over other city agencies is misaligned with its charter role, and the proposed shared enforcement with the Conflicts of Interest Board would create complexity and inconsistent standards.
chapters.title: Melillo says CFB cannot support T2026-2554's shared enforcement structure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Lastly, T2026-2554, introduced by Councilmember Feliz, would require

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: government agencies to disclose their partnerships on certain third-party public communications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: As currently drafted, the bill raises fundamental concerns that prevent the CFB from supporting it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Designating the CFB as an enforcing agency is misaligned with our current charter role, our existing role and charter mandate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: The CFB does not investigate or regulate other city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: The proposed shared enforcement structure with the Conflicts of Interest Board compounds this problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Dividing responsibility between two agencies would create unnecessary complexity in rulemaking, enforcement procedures, and administration, potentially producing inconsistent standards and undermining effective enforcement.

chapters.summary: Melillo says the CFB's influencer program effectively reaches voters traditional outreach misses, backed by nonpartisanship safeguards, and that the agency is prepared to share operational and regulatory expertise as the Council considers the bills.
chapters.title: Melillo concludes CFB influencer program is effective with strong safeguards

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Without significant changes to the proposed enforcement structure, the CFB cannot support this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: In conclusion, we strongly believe the CFB's influencer program is an effective tool for reaching voters whom traditional outreach methods do not effectively engage, backed by strong safeguards to protect the agency's nonpartisanship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: The CFB also approaches this issue as the regulator responsible for advising campaigns on their disclosure obligations and enforcing their misuse, and we are committed to providing clear guidance that reflects our existing disclosure requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: The agency is prepared to share its operational and regulatory expertise as the Council considers these issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: We remain committed to strengthening our local democracy, and we look forward to working together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: to ensure New Yorkers receive transparent information about political content, no matter how the content reaches them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: And I welcome your questions.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how the CFB decides which influencers to work with and how campaigns differ from traditional media; Melillo explains younger audiences distrust traditional advertising and prefer authentic content, and describes bringing selection in-house with a social media manager identifying NYC-based non-political creators like Public Opinion and Righteous Eats.
chapters.title: Brewer asks Melillo how CFB selects influencers and differs from traditional media

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Just a few.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you decide which influencers you want to work with?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What is the difference between campaigns you create with these influencers and those created for traditional media?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then also, I think you have said that you have brought your influencer campaign in-house.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I didn't know what that meant.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Those are my three questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: I'm going to actually step back and answer the second one first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So when we're thinking about reaching younger voters, what traditional advertising generally looks like is some sort of branded campaign asset that is professionally designed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: It usually has a field-tested message attached to it, a call to action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: And you can generally tell what these advertisements look like pretty clearly in the subways or whenever you're seeing it out in the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: I think what research has pretty consistently shown, especially for younger people who just have been incessantly targeted by ads from the time they were children,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: is that they are increasingly suspicious of traditional advertising and prefer content that feels more authentic to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So this is why you've really seen the rise of influencer partnerships and advertising, because in these sorts of short-form content, influencers are creating posts or making videos, or it's really just someone to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: talking to a camera or maybe posting some words, and it seems like it's coming from a person as opposed to an organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So I would say a number of agencies, not just the Campaign Finance Board, have been experimenting more with this type of, these types of ways to reach voters, especially for the past five to six years, as a lot more of our work has sort of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: migrated online as these generational changes occur.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So when we are going out, and what I mean by when I said we brought that work in-house,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: before we were paying an advertising agency, which was at the time Miller Advertising, we aren't currently working with them, and they sort of went out and identified some potential influencers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: We have a social media manager in-house, as many government agencies do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: And our social media manager actually began doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: As someone who is much more online as I am, I admit, she began doing the work of really looking at who are New York City-based influencers that don't make content that's political in nature, but it's very New York City-specific.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So we have, you know, we've partnered with outlets such as Public Opinion, who does like man-on-the-street style interviews.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: We've partnered with the influencer behind Righteous Eats, who like profiles mom and pop shops and eateries around, especially the outer boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: People who aren't necessarily creating content that is political.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: political in nature, or even civically engaged, but have an interest in the outcomes of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So generally that is like our first cut of who are New York City content creators who live in the five boroughs and their audiences are in the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: And then from there,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: we start to winnow down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Our social media team will sort of do a review of what are the types of things that they've posted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Do we think that this would be an appropriate content creator for the campaign finance board to partner with?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Have they posted political content in the past that could be seen as partisan in a way we don't necessarily want to be associated with?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: You know, sometimes they're content creators, depending on what they do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Maybe they've posted things that aren't suitable for work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Maybe we shouldn't partner with them as a government agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: But for the most part, we will sort of come up with a short list and then go from there and then ask ourselves,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Is anyone on this list, or do we need to find additional people who are reaching out to our priority audiences, especially in-language audiences or people that are harder to reach?

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how the CFB determines disclosure language and hashtags; Melillo says the CFB currently follows each platform's political advertising rules but is reviewing whether its disclosure standards should match paid-for-by notice standards for greater consistency.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about disclosure language and hashtags; Melillo says CFB is reviewing standards

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And do you use certain language, hashtags, or whatever for disclosure?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So maybe that's something other agencies should pay more attention to.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you determine that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: One of the things we've been discussing internally as a result of this hearing, because right now we follow the practices required by each of the platforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: They all have slightly different rules depending.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: especially for political advertising, there's like a verification process that everyone has to go through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So we go through that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: But one of the things I think we're currently looking at is our disclosure standards meeting the same standards as like a paid for by notice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Because I think that we could probably be more consistent at using those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: As someone who I tend to see a lot of this content, both before it goes out and organically and non-organically,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: it's generally pretty clear when we've partnered with a content creator, but I think this is just a good opportunity for us to sort of do a review and make sure it's as clear as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanta Smith-Cruz
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Wong.

chapters.summary: Wong says traditional reporters ask tough questions while influencers repeat talking points, which is propaganda, and his bill aims to ensure the public knows content is paid for with tax dollars; Melillo distinguishes the elections part of the charter from the public officials' use of resources section and says CFB rules already cover campaign disclaimers.
chapters.title: Wong explains his bill's intent and asks whether CFB rules cover influencers

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I just wanted to tell you the spirit of my bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: See, traditional reporters, they come to City Hall, they talk, they ask questions, tough questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like even to me or to the mayor, to the public advocate, and we get challenged.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And that's the way it worked with traditional media.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And they do not simply take the city horse talking points and repeat them.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And it appears to me that's what the influencers are doing.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And that's not, to me, that's not news.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: That's propaganda.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So the spirit of my bill is that when the public sees these messages,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They have the right to know this is paid for, paid by our tax dollars.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And though no one's running a campaign, or if the mayor's doing this, or if I'm doing this right now, we're not running a campaign, but the public has to know.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my question to you is, you seem to say that this is already covered by existing laws of campaign finance board, but I don't see it that covers influencers.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can you talk about that?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And then I'll lead to my part two of my question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Let me draw a distinction between two separate parts of the charter, because what your bill would modify, and that's T2026-2553, what that would modify is the elections part of the charter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: specific to elections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So what that would not cover is what City Hall is doing with influencers that is the issue for the hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: The other three pieces of legislation being considered would modify a different section of the charter, which is about public officials'use of resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: And that's where you find the 90-day mailing blackout provision that elected officials must follow before an election.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So when we're saying, and it's not that we disagree with the spirit or the intent of your bill, we're just saying it's already covered in our rules, and we don't necessarily feel like the charter has to be amended to reflect it because it is covered in our rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: And I'll just state this very quickly as like a matter of something we always consider when we're thinking about what needs to go in the charter or the admin code or in the CFB rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Generally, I think it's okay to direct the CFB to do things at a high level, but not get super specific about the way technology works because it changes so quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So the way this would regulate paid-for-by notices, which is the way our rules currently regulate it, that could become a very stale piece of the charter if something about the social media platforms were to change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So, for example, there's a requirement for paid-for-by notifications in the comments section.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: What if Instagram removed comments?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: or the ability to add comments to posts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Then we would have to think about what is a different sort of disclosure regime that we would advise campaigns, but that section of the charter would become out of date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So generally, we like to align on the intent of things and then have these conversations about where we think it should go and what the CFB should be directed to do.

chapters.summary: Wong says the line between propaganda and news is blurring with AI graphics and asks whether missing disclaimers are an enforcement problem or a gap; Melillo explains the CFB regulates the mayor's campaign but not his activities as mayor or City Hall staff carrying out public duties, so the bill would not regulate current City Hall content.
chapters.title: Wong asks whether disclaimers are an enforcement problem or a gap

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yes, and as I see it, it's becoming, there's a very blurry line now between propaganda and news.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It seems to me that the public is perceiving it that way, and that concerns me, especially with the use of AI graphics, the videos of...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Of a mass crowd listening in to somebody making an announcement in public.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So those are concerning and those are misleading and they can be abused.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So the spirit of my bill is to clearly identify these messages that are created by influencers or they're subcontractors of some PR firm.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Hired by the administration, you know, that the public needs to know that it's one, it's like AI created, or two, it's paid by our tax dollars, right?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So that's where I'm coming from now.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What you're saying that this is already covered, but I don't see these disclaimers.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: In social media videos that's used by pretty much everybody, not just the mayor's office.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So are we dealing with...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: with an enforcement problem or we're dealing with gaps that we are addressing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: I will answer this as an example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: The Campaign Finance Board regulates the mayor's campaign and his activities on his campaign for office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: We do not regulate the mayor's activities or the activities of any city hall staffer in carrying out their public duties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: So this bill would actually not regulate the content of what City Hall is doing right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: It would regulate what campaigns are doing.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So what you're telling me is that once the campaign is over, these propaganda videos are not governed by the campaign finance board.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: If these videos were created as a result of the campaign, so if the campaign had paid an influencer to create videos on the campaign's behalf, that would be regulated campaign spending.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: But once it's no longer associated with the campaign, it becomes something that we don't have regulatory oversight over.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for making that clarification.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Brewer thanks Melillo, dismisses the CFB panel, and opens public testimony, reminding the public that decorum must be preserved, no video recording is allowed, speakers get three minutes, and written testimony can be submitted to the sergeant at arms or by email within 72 hours.
chapters.title: Brewer dismisses CFB panel and opens public testimony

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much for you, and you are dismissed.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And we look forward to working with CFB, always.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Melillo
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Dr.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Anya Schiffman, who is the author of the Columbia Journalism Review, the article that is of much discussion and respected.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So this is part of the public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's what we're opening now.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I remind members of the public, this is a government proceeding.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Decorum shall be reserved.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You will remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The witness table is for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the sergeant if you want to.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If you want to speak, make sure you fill out an appearance card with the sergeant and be recognized, and you'll have three minutes to talk on today's hearing topic, but I'm sure the doctor can have some more time.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And if you have a written statement or additional, you can submit it to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You also can send written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of the close, not audio and video.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And anybody who's got a, in person, you'll come up to the table when you're called, and we will call those from Zoom if they are there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And thank you for being here, and congratulations on your article.

chapters.summary: Dr. Anya Schiffrin, Senior Lecturer at Columbia's School of International and Public Affairs, introduces her forthcoming paper 'Mapping New York City Influencers and the Funding of Public Messaging,' noting the working paper is online and the final version will be published by the Tao Center for Digital Journalism with an October 19 launch event.
chapters.title: Dr. Anya Schiffrin introduces her Columbia research on NYC influencers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: This is my first hearing ever in my life, so I just want to make sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I have written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I was not expecting to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Is there time for me to do both, read my written testimony?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have a long list of questions for you here, so go right ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Okay, here we go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the opportunity to submit written testimony about my forthcoming paper, Mapping New York City Influencers and the Funding of Public Messaging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: A working paper version, which is 11,000 words, is already available online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I am Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Anya Shiffrin, Senior Lecturer in Discipline at Columbia University School of International and Public Affairs, and I'm the author of this working paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: The final version will be published as a policy brief by the Tao Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia University.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: We're having an event on October 19th to launch the paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I think it will be open to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I've devoted much of my academic career to the study of information ecosystems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I have long been preoccupied with questions about how citizens can receive quality information and what the obstacles are to receiving that information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I've edited three volumes on media capture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I've written a PhD dissertation on policies to address mis- and disinformation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I've studied government policies to support journalism, and I've made recommendations on how government and philanthropy can support the provision of quality information while respecting editorial independence and press freedom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Over the years, I've organized many conferences bringing together government officials from all over the world with philanthropists, and I do believe that on the subject that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: that we're tackling today, there is a huge amount that can be learned from Canada, from the European Union, and from other countries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And at the end of my testimony, I have two pages of comparative policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I think there's a lot that we can be talking about apart from the signal group.

chapters.summary: Schiffrin explains governments must communicate policies to citizens amid AI slop and fragmented news habits, citing France, Canada, and the U.S. paying influencers for health, voting, and climate messaging, Health and Hospitals' pandemic work, MTA celebrity announcements, and new pilot programs under the Mamdani administration.
chapters.title: Schiffrin describes government use of influencers for public information

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Anyway, because of my concern about information,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: and public information, I decided to spend the summer researching influencers who provide information to New Yorkers about city services, laws, and policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: As we know well in the communications field, it's not enough for governments to pass laws and implement policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: It's necessary to communicate those policies to citizens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And this task has gotten ever harder in a world of AI slop, information overload, and fragmented habits of news consumption.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I note in my paper that government agencies have long tried to provide trusted information to citizens about the services that governments provide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: In France, Canada, and the U.S., social media influencers are sometimes paid to disseminate information about health care, voting, climate change, and to reach young audiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I also talked about the pandemic when health and hospitals began using influencers to remind people to get tested and then to get vaccines when they were available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: The MTA has used celebrities to record public announcements about the subways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And we just heard from the Campaign Finance Board about some of their efforts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I'm happy to talk about my research project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: The Campaign Finance Board were the only agency using influencers that was willing to give me extensive on-the-record discussion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And I really appreciated the comments made by the previous person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: The sanitation department hired a marketing firm, Karen Pace, to work with New York Nico as part of its campaign to remind New Yorkers not to litter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: They received a grant, the sanitation department, to spread the word about composting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And since Mamdani's taken office, there's started to be pilot programs aimed at using influencers on Instagram and TikTok to promote city services such as pre-K, public budgeting processes, which we talked about earlier, and tenants'rights, which also came up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs recently announced a new information campaign that will include content creators and influencers.

chapters.summary: Schiffrin says the city works with advertising and marketing agencies under citywide media placement contracts that identify and hire influencers, issue contracts and payments, and monitor impact, but there is secrecy around hiring and payment, no systemic record keeping of content creators, and unclear regulations.
chapters.title: Schiffrin describes city media contracts and lack of record keeping

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Where I think it's important to take a real close look is the City of New York works with a group of advertising and marketing agencies that place advertisements on behalf of city agencies and manage influencer relationships

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: under the citywide media placement contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: This relationship management can include identifying and hiring influencers, issuing contracts and payments, working with the influencers on the content they deliver, and monitoring the impact of that content.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Some information is available in City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: documents online, but in general there's quite a bit of secrecy regarding the hiring and payment of these messengers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: There is no systemic record keeping that we could find of the content creators hired by city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And we found that, just as we saw today, that many of the regulations governing influence relationships are unknown and unclear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: We found a lack of standards as to disclosure and transparency and a lack of knowledge about what laws, if any, apply.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And this, by the way, seems to be a universal problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: When the EU did a sweep of influencers a couple years ago, I cite that in my paper, they also found that mostly people didn't know what the laws were and were not following the disclosure laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So this is not just us.

chapters.summary: Schiffrin says labeling of paid influencer content is inconsistent, citing Spain's rule requiring 'paid for' visible throughout videos rather than 'partner' or 'collab,' and notes the EU found influencers largely unaware of disclosure laws, suggesting work can be done to strengthen disclosure and transparency.
chapters.title: Schiffrin notes inconsistent labeling and international disclosure standards

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: We mentioned in our paper that we also found that labeling of the paid influencer content seems to be inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: We note in the paper some of the different hashtags we saw, and we note countries like Spain basically have very clear rule.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: It has to say paid for, can't say partner, can't say collab, has to be visible throughout the video.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I think there's work that can be done on strengthening disclosure and transparency of this paid work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And then as we were, during the course of our research, and I'll say by the way that, you know, I was working with Wyatt, who's an undergrad at Columbia College, and he was the chief researcher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I had a couple of other students helping.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I thought when I was starting the paper that I would be really writing about a comparative look at regulation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And then what I found was that there were

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: so little information available about what was happening in New York that actually my contribution to the field would be simply trying to map.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So we have parts that we haven't published yet because we haven't, you know, we're not sure how accurate they are, but we tried to pull out from the budget records different information about the different contracts.

chapters.summary: Schiffrin says her team pulled together a list of more than 200 influencers but is not yet confident enough to release it, hopes the hearings will prompt more information from the city, and offers to help draft disclosure and transparency legislation and connect officials with international counterparts.
chapters.title: Schiffrin describes mapping over 200 influencers and seeking more city information

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: We included a sidebar on who the agencies are, and we have pulled together a list of more than 200 influencers, but we're not yet happy enough about it to release it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So we do have a lot of stuff that still feels a little rough to us, and I'm so much hoping that now that these hearings are happening that perhaps more information will be forthcoming from the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
