utterances.text: And like you, you know, I need to finish this paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: It's got to get published and presented in the middle of October.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So anybody who can talk to us and provide more information, we would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And it goes without saying that we'd be really delighted to help with the drafting of legislation, focusing on disclosure and transparency, and connecting you to officials around the world who have already done this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: There's a lot out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So that's something I wanted to say.

chapters.summary: Schiffrin says the Signal group has characteristics of a press list but differs, is unpaid per Amelia Rowland's office, and raises questions about the intake process for influencers versus press passes, and why a separate Signal group exists rather than one press list for everyone.
chapters.title: Schiffrin analyzes the Signal group's function and access questions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And then, yeah, so we sort of stumbled on the signal group.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And we were very interested in the communications field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: We talk a lot about boundary work, what's different about a journalist from an influencer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I was really trying to understand the sort of contours of what this signal group actually was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: It has characteristics of a press list, but in other ways it seems very different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: It seems that this group is not paid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: They were very clear about that from Amelia Rowland's office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And there's been, I would say, there's three things that I find sort of important or concerning about this group.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I think we focused a lot today on the need for record retention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So clearly I won't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I would say that there's sort of a lack of clarity as to the precise function of the unpaid influencers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And, you know, is the relationship between City Hall and influencers a sort of standard journalist?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Press relationship to get a city hall press pass you need to fill out a lot of forms you need to demonstrate the air covering you know what exactly is the intake process um and then a third question

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: when i when i my previous life when i was a journalist i wrote quite a bit about regulation fd which was issued by the securities and exchange commission

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: in 2000 and that required that material information be made public to all relevant parties at the same time and not given in advance to favored analysts or investors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And as I recall, the Wall Street Journal was actually against that law because they like getting things first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So one of the things I've been puzzling over is why would there be a need for a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Separate signal group as opposed to a press list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I'm very interested in that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you just have one list for everybody and have a kind of, you know, a process for everybody to join it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So that's one of the research questions that has remained unanswered.

chapters.summary: Schiffrin says she sent dozens of emails to City Hall and agencies since July without answers, unlike her experience with EU officials, and that after her paper came out Rowland texted her saying the Signal group information is the same as the regular press list, usually just links to press releases and livestreams.
chapters.title: Schiffrin describes unanswered emails and Rowland's response on Signal content

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I sent dozens of emails to different parts of City Hall and to city agencies since July asking for information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: When I did my PhD on disinformation, Google and Facebook didn't speak to me once in the years I was doing my research, but every single official

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: or government employee that I wrote to at the EU Commission or the EU Parliament met with me for at least an hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I'm very used to engaging with government officials as part of my academic research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And I was a little surprised when I didn't get an answer from anybody at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So after the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Paper came out, I did get a text message from Amelia Rowland and, you know, re-sent many of the questions I've been sending since July.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So on Saturday, she sent me a text message about this particular question in which she said that the information in the signal group is not different at all from the information given to the regular press list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Quote, it is usually just a link to a press release and link to the announcement live stream on YouTube, Roland said in a text message on September 21st.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: But I'm looking forward to further clarification.

chapters.summary: Schiffrin notes City Hall's Signal group is part of a broader trend including the Pentagon hiring conservative military influencers, corporate and foreign interests working with influencers, and Qatar and Israel spending on pro-Trump influencers, arguing regulation is important.
chapters.title: Schiffrin places Signal group in broader global influencer trend

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And then I just also note that City Hall's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Use of a signal group to reach content creators is part of a broader trend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: In August, journalists revealed that the Pentagon had hired conservative military influencers, apparently to amplify messages of Defense Secretary Pete Hesgett.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: January 11th article in the Wall Street Journal talked about corporate and foreign interests working with influencers to push their agendas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: One example cited in the article is the government of Qatar giving free trips to Doha and perks to a group of pro-Trump influencers and also planned spending of $900,000 by Israel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I don't know if that's government or who in Israel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And direct payments to influencers from companies in the solar and health industries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So this is part of a larger trend, which I think is why regulation is so important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And, you know, at least our mayor is not ripping up federal documents and putting them in the toilet when we talk about record retention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So, you know, that's something.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I do think that all the media coverage about the use of influencers to promote political agendas or candidates, Ken Bensinger has done a terrific job at the New York Times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I was fortunate enough to talk to Emma Goldberg after I'd written my first paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And all of this coverage has really raised questions about what kind of regulations are needed.

chapters.summary: Schiffrin recommends clear disclosure of influencer relationships applying to paid and unpaid content, standardized visible hashtags like Spain's 'paid partnership,' regular publication of influencer lists, in-house training for employees and vendors, and an influencer hub modeled on the EU and FTC.
chapters.title: Schiffrin recommends disclosure, labeling, and training standards

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And so a lot of what I'm seeing globally is disclosure and labeling of influencer content.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And that has begun to attract the attention of regulators in the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And overseas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I think that there's, given the amount of online violence and physical threats in the real world to journalists and influencers, I think that there's a fear of naming who the influencers are, for example, in the signal group.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: But I think we need to weigh that against the pollution of the information ecosystem and the mistrust created when audiences are not aware of the alliances or the agendas of the people that they encounter online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: You know, I have great hope that New York could really be a standard setter for a lot of this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I think there's no reason we couldn't do sort of world first or standard setting in terms of research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I mean, in terms of regulation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So some of the recommendations I made, and I'm very open to revising them if it turns out we don't need them or we already have them, but I would argue for a clear disclosure of relationships with influencers, ideally applying to both paid and unpaid content.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I think standardized disclosure, as just came up, and I was very glad to hear the Campaign Finance Board is thinking about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So consistent use of hashtags, maybe at the top of the videos, remain throughout the video, be visible at all times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And it should be clear, again, what Spain has done of labeling things paid partnership as opposed to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Collaboration and again some sort of label or disclosure for unpaid but persistent relationships.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: That should also be visible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I certainly think that some kind of regular publication of lists of influencers who work with the city agencies and explain what this consists of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: As I mentioned, it seems to all go through marketing agencies that don't seem to provide information or answer questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And another time I hope we can talk about city advertising because, again, Canada, Sweden, UK, there are many countries that have very strong guidelines on city advertising, and I would love us to maybe look at that as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I also think that the mayor's office should probably publicize the disclosure rules far more completely

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: and provide in-house training for city employees, vendors, and marketing agencies that work with influencers, as well as training for influencers, agency staff, employees working with influencers, and vending and marketing firms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I think it's very important, especially for new hires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: When you have a new administration, you may have people coming in who don't know the rules, so have to kind of make sure they're clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Maybe the mayor's office could create a sort of influencer hub the same way the EU has done, and the FTC pages are actually very helpful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: They provide clearly written information and ethical guidelines regarding content and information on regulations that cover influencers and best practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And then I have this table of the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Regulatory landscape and some of the European.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Regulations as I mentioned I'm still working on this so I'm very open for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: you know, more information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Very happy to, you know, bring experts together, convene, and keep discussing all of this.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether England, the EU, or Canada use Signal or communicate differently; Schiffrin says the Signal group was an accidental finding and her research focused on influencers promoting government programs, noting Canada debates whether influencers must be paid to require disclosure and what the threshold should be.
chapters.title: Brewer asks Schiffrin about other countries' communication practices

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: When you're talking about England or EU or any of those other Canada, are they also using a signal or other type of communication, do you know, or is it done differently?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So the research that I was doing, I mean, the signal group was sort of an accidental finding for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: The research that I was doing was actually on influencers who are promoting information about government programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And what's so interesting about some of this, I was just looking at Canada, you know, one of the debates is, do the influencers need to be paid in order to be told to disclose?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I think that would be a real question for us, you know, is what is our bar?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Is it number of followers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Is it how often you're posting?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Is it how much money you're making?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Is it whether you're getting a gift or a trip?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Is it, you know, the actual content of the message?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I think all of those will need to be sort of considered when you think about regulation.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what Schiffrin means by disclosures of persistent relationships; Schiffrin explains journalists covering City Hall apply for press passes, and asks whether groups regularly receiving and reporting information are like journalists and whether some registration or training requirement should apply, noting the U.S. tradition against licensing.
chapters.title: Brewer asks what persistent relationship disclosures mean

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What do you mean by disclosures of persistent relationships?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So, again, as I mentioned, you know, journalists that cover City Hall have a press pass, which they apply for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So if there are groups of people that are getting information on a regular basis and then reporting out that information, are they like the journalists?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Do we need to then think?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: about some sort of, you know, traditionally in this country, press freedom groups, newspapers, the profession has been very much against licensing, whereas in Europe you would have rules about, you know, did you go to this journalism school?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: How much training have you had?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Then you can get a press pass.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: That has not been the American way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: But I think, as someone mentioned earlier, you know, this is new forms of communication, and so clearly regulation hasn't caught up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I think these are all things we can really think about.

chapters.summary: Wong says traditional media and influencers appear to get different press statements and that influencers sometimes get information first, asking whether they should have equal access; Schiffrin says this is 'anecdata' and that Rowland told her influencers get the same press releases as journalists, calling for further study.
chapters.title: Wong asks whether influencers and traditional media have equal access

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question is access.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like traditional media, it seemed to me that they're getting the different set of press statements from, say, from the mayor's office.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: While the influencers getting a separate set of feeds from Emilia Roland.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So it seemed to me they don't have equal access.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And some, I even heard that the influencers got hold of information way before the...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Traditional reporters did.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my question is, should they have equal access if there's any activity coming from the mayor's office?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And why are they not getting the same access?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Yes, well, I think you raise a very important point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And, you know, in academia, we would call this anecdata.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: We don't have a full, you know, we don't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: don't have a full picture of what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: We have anecdotes that are certainly concerning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I was told, I think it was by Hamad in a text message, that there are more briefings for journalists than there are for influencers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And I was just told Saturday by Amelia in a text message that basically the influencers are given the same press releases as journalists.

chapters.summary: Wong says he saw videos of the mayor promoting ballot proposals, which should be labeled as political messages paid for by taxpayers, and that with so many influencers someone is getting paid; Schiffrin says Rowland's position is that Signal group members are not paid for being in the group, but whether some have city contracts needs clarification.
chapters.title: Wong raises ballot proposal videos and paid influencer concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I think this would be an area for further study and clarification.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And before coming to this hearing, I'm watching the videos of the mayor promoting a ballot issue on these ballot proposals.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And that is, to me, not news that you're promoting politics.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You're telling voters.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: About an issue they will be voting on in November, and that should clearly be indicated that that is a political message, and it should clearly say it is paid by the tax dollars of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And I don't think so many influencers work for free.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So it seemed to me that with so many of them out there, you know, somebody's getting paid and we're watching these propagandists.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And it's hard to distinguish them from news.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that comment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I mean, I think that the position of Amelia Rowland is that none of the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: those influencers on the signal group are getting paid for being on that signal group.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: You know, whether some of them at some times are wearing other hats and perhaps getting that $5,000 contract with the city agency needs clarification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: I know that everybody's been sitting here for hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: You don't really need to listen to an academic drone on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: But we did a report for the government of Bhutan years ago about advertising in newspapers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And we studied, I think it was six different countries, to look at their regulations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: And there are exactly what you're saying, a lot of guidelines about, you know, when can images appear of the mayor?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: When can they back certain things?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: How close to an election?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: Should they be making a statement?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: How do you make sure that you're actually giving people information like...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: You know, enroll your kid in kindergarten versus sort of say, hey, we're doing a great job, vote for us.

chapters.summary: Brewer says New York City rules on election-adjacent communications are well articulated but not always enforced, and Wong says the public may not distinguish flu shot reminders from political propaganda about ballot proposals, arguing the distinction must be defined and labeled as paid for by taxpayers.
chapters.title: Brewer and Wong discuss enforcement gaps on ballot question communications

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anya Schiffrin
utterances.text: So I think that, sorry, as an academic, I think we have to have a separate conversation about those regulations and guidelines because it's complex and there's a lot of examples from around the world.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just want to say, having done this for many years, those are usually in New York City very well articulated, to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: However.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're not always enforced.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So there is that we heard earlier from the agencies that many of the bills are good, but they already exist.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We don't have, in my opinion, that's my opinion, not a great enforcement, particularly on these ballot questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I can go on and on about what you are or not.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: supposed to do at different times.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, oversight is tough.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are you, any more?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Quickly.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Again, the public may not be sophisticated, able to distinguish, oh, that is a message reminding me to take flu shots or from that is a political propaganda telling me about

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: these ballot proposals in November hinting that which way I should vote.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So I think that distinction has to be defined and has to be clearly specified that is paid for by the tax dollars, taxpayers of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And right now it doesn't look like it, okay?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: As we approach the election day, I think we'll be seeing more and more of these videos.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And that is dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We look forward to continuing to work with you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The next panel is Rachel Fowles, Susan Lerner, and Grace Rao.

chapters.summary: Brewer thanks Schiffrin and calls the next panel: Rachel Fauss, Susan Lerner, and Grace Rauh, with Ben also invited to come up.
chapters.title: Brewer calls next panel of good government groups

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And if Ben wants to come up also, is that what you're doing?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You can come up, Ben.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're always up.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead, whoever wants to start.

chapters.summary: Rachael Fauss of Reinvent Albany asks the Council to pass legislation clarifying that all electronic communications creating a public record, including instant messages, be archived and retrievable by FOIL officers, and to advance an influencer disclosure bill modeled on FTC rules through the contracting process.
chapters.title: Reinvent Albany's Rachael Fauss recommends records retention and influencer disclosure bills

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: Thanks for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: My name is Rachel Foss.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: I'm the Senior Policy Advisor for Reinvent Albany.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: We advocate for transparent and accountable government in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: I'm going to just run through our basic recommendations, and I might spend a little more time on the records issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: So first, we ask the council to pass legislation clarifying that all electronic communications that results in the creation of a public record, including instant messages, be archived and easily retrievable by agency FOIL officers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: I'll talk a little bit more about the draft bill we put together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: Second, the council should move forward with a new influencer disclosure bill modeled after current FTC rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: And this should be done through the city contracting process rather than some of the means outlined in the legislation today.

chapters.summary: Fauss asks the Council to revise T2026-2555 and T2026-1440 to incorporate expert perspectives and not to move forward with T2026-2554 and T2026-2553 due to CFB concerns, and argues the DORIS policy's transitory framing is backwards since instant messages are often records.
chapters.title: Fauss recommends revising two bills and opposing two others

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: We asked the council to revise T-2026-2555, that's the blackout period bill,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: and T-2026-1440, the third-party communication reporting, to incorporate the perspectives of the experts here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: And then we asked the council not to move forward with...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: 2445 and 2, I'm sorry, 2554 and 2553 because of some of the concerns of the CFB.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: raised. On the records retention issue, I think the bill we've put together would answer a lot of the questions that you had, Gail, in particular.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: transitory.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: The Doris policy talks about transitory as it's almost presupposing that an instant message would never be a record and we think that's a bit backwards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: I would suggest we define instant messages as substantive and non-substantive and take transitory out of it because in reality we know that those messages are records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: They contain

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: information that should be retained.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: I want to just have a clarification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: Doris does have a role in deletion policy under the charter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: They are supposed to approve whether messages are deleted or not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: I'm sorry, records are deleted or not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: So our draft bill would also make sure that instant messages are part of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: So I know my time is out, but I think the draft legislation we put in this testimony and that I know we shared with you in advance, I think would address many of the problems that were raised today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: And we look forward to talking with you more about that.

chapters.summary: Grace Rauh, Executive Director of Citizens Union, says auto-delete functions should be explicitly prohibited from official city business, citing her experience suing the de Blasio administration for emails involving outside political advisors, and notes WhatsApp and Slack also add auto-delete functions.
chapters.title: Citizens Union's Grace Rauh calls for banning auto-delete functions

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you for waiting.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead, Nick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Brewer and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: My name is Grace Rao.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: I'm the executive director of Citizens Union, a nonpartisan good government and democracy organization that has been working for honest, accountable, effective government, fair and open elections, and a civically engaged public for nearly 130 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: I want to start by thanking you for calling this important oversight hearing, and I want to address the two main separate issues before the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: First on Signal and the idea of auto-delete apps and messaging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: We believe that this is a clear black and white issue with a simple policy solution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: Automatic delete functions should be explicitly prohibited from any official city business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: I know firsthand from my time as a reporter at New York One, obtaining government records can sometimes require significant effort, but ultimately deserve to be in the public realm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: I successfully sued the de Blasio administration to obtain emails involving outside political advisors and fought City Hall's efforts to keep those records from public scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: The growing use of instant messaging applications does create challenges because it's not just on one app like Signal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: We're seeing WhatsApp, Slack, other platforms that are creating and adding auto-delete functions that make it more difficult to ensure that government records are retained and available to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: Doris does strongly discourage use of instant messaging for substantive conversations, but the existing policies do not go far enough, and it's necessary for the city to establish clear technology-neutral rules in the charter

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: prohibiting government employees from using auto-delete functions for government communications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: There's a basic principle that should be upheld here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: City employees cannot use or permit the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: use of any function that automatically deletes or destroys a government record after a fixed period of time.

chapters.summary: Rauh says paid government advertising including influencer content must be publicly disclosed, that FTC rules requiring clear and conspicuous disclosure of paid relationships should be incorporated into city advertising contracts with a uniform citywide standard, and that unpaid influencer engagement is fine but should not come at the expense of reporter access.
chapters.title: Rauh calls for FTC-style influencer disclosure in city advertising contracts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: And then on the second piece, the idea of paid government advertising, including influencer content, it needs to be publicly disclosed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: Others have mentioned the Federal Trade Commission has rules establishing influencers to clearly and conspicuously disclose paid relationships.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: That is needed here, and we believe that that requirement should be incorporated into the city's advertising contracts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: and that there should be a uniform citywide standard rather than leaving this up to individual agencies or contractors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: There's more details on both in my written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: But finally, on the question of unpaid influencers, we want to make it clear that there is nothing inherently wrong with City Hall communicating its actions, programs, or achievements to unpaid influencers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: Social media content creators are now a permanent part of the communications landscape.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: We know elected officials will continue to use them to communicate with the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: We want to note that that engagement should not come at the expense of reporter access, press scrutiny, as we are seeing in Washington, D.C.,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: and City Hall should not be providing influencers with any confidential information or privileged access to information in exchange for favorable coverage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Rauh
utterances.text: But we believe the city's existing ethic laws address.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: those concerns.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Susan Lerner, Executive Director of Common Cause New York, focuses on the hearing's civic engagement title, citing academic definitions and noting that OME's website emphasizes tenant organizing rather than broader information about accessing city government, questioning whether the city should pick particular types of organizing.
chapters.title: Common Cause's Susan Lerner questions what civic engagement means for the city

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: I'm Susan Lerner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Director of Common Cause New York, and I too want to thank the Chair and the Committee for this hearing, which I think covers a lot of very important areas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: I would like to focus on something that hasn't been fully discussed, I think, in as great detail as I would like, which is the title is the Mamdani Administration Civic Engagement Efforts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: And I think we need to be talking about what does it mean for the city to be involved in civic engagement?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: What is civic engagement?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: What is the appropriate?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: Use of city resources and what is the goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: Academic definitions of civic engagement say that civic engagement means working to make a difference in the civic life of our communities and developing the combination of knowledge, skills, values, and motivation to make that difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: And I was struck in the testimony from the commissioner of the Office of Mass Engagement of how fluidly she has incorporated

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: a lot of the terminology about civic engagement, but that virtually all of her examples of the city, her

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: division, I would call it, her office's civic engagement, were really performed by the smaller agency, the smaller offices within that umbrella.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: already existed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: And when I went to the office of Mass Engagement's website, I was struck by the difference in how they are communicating on their website what they do with how she described what they do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: Because rather than talking about basic information of how to access or understand city government, it's very narrow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: It's all about tenant organizing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: And so we're not having the basic discussion of what is civic engagement and what should the city be fostering?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: Should it be picking a particular type of organizing or should it be a broader?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: Invitation to our residents to understand government and to affect it, whatever policies the individual thinks is a good idea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: And some of that is happening, the Civic Engagement Commission, some of the outreach around benefits, but I would suggest that the outlook of the Office of Mass Engagement is actually different than what was testified here.

chapters.summary: Lerner suggests disclosure stating communication was initiated by or in partnership with the City of New York so residents know whether content is independent or results from talking points, which she agrees are substantive communications, and says Common Cause's written testimony offers amendments to strengthen the bills.
chapters.title: Lerner proposes disclosure for ongoing influencer relationships

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: I would briefly like to say that when we're talking about influencers, I think we do need some disclosure about the ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: Relationship and we suggest that a disclosure that says communication initiated by the city of New York or partnership with the city of New York provides information that the resident that the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: taker of the social media needs to know

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: Is this really an independent communication, or does it result from suggestions like talking points, which are clearly, I agree,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: substantive communications, however they are communicated to the social media communicators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: And our testimony has extensive suggestions for amendments and improvements to the bills, which we generally support, but we feel should be strengthened in specific ways that we detail in our written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Lerner
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Wong says his bill aims to close the gap so the public knows content like ballot proposal videos or OME door-knocking is not news, and asks Reinvent Albany about its recommendation not to move the bill; Fauss says the charter section being amended covers independent expenditure disclosures, which are a national model, and suggests the bill may need changes to regulate different activity.
chapters.title: Wong asks panel about his bill's intent to label paid political messaging

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: A question for the panel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We already heard from CFB that they will oversight campaign money being spent on

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: influencers and on pushing for an agenda while we do not see that as news.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But my question is, my bill...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Is trying to fix this when the mayor is using tax dollars to promote his agenda, rather than treating it as a piece of news,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: just like the ballot proposal videos I've seen, or videos of the Office of Mass Engagement knocking door to door, telling tenants,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: about the unions out there and then they could join.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's not news.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the public has to know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And my question to you is that, well, to reinvent Albany is that you wrote here that you don't want, with the council should not move the bill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But my spirit of the bill is to close this gap and let the public know that what they're watching is not news.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Let's get our answer.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yes, please answer that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: I think I, having listened to the CFB, I think the way they put it is right, that, you know, the part of the chapter, the charter you're amending is about the independent expenditure disclosures, which we are very, very sensitive about as

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: the New York City has model independent expenditure disclosure rules with the paid for by.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: And I think your intent is for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: The mayor's activity while in office, not as a candidate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: And we don't want to see changes to the IE disclosures, the paid for by disclosures that affect campaigns because they are very strong in CFB as, like I said, as a national model on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: So I think if your intent is to regulate different activity, you know, maybe the bill needs a change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: But I understand your point that the public deserves more information, and we absolutely do support paid-for-by disclosures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: As I mentioned, we think that it could be done through the contracting process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: The FTC rules are one way to look at it, but it's, I think your goals are similar to ours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: I just think the app,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: application in the bill the way it's drafted is where we had some concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachael Fauss
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you, Jim.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We appreciate this, and we will go to the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brewer calls the next panel: Charles Diamond, Octavio Blanco, and Tony Rossum, inviting whoever would like to go first.
chapters.title: Brewer calls panel of community media and content creators

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We've got Charles Diamond, Octavio Blanco, and Tony Rossum.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you all, whomever would like to go first.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you for being here.

chapters.summary: Octavio Blanco, executive editor of Uptown Voices in Washington Heights, denies media accusations that his outlet was paid to cover Mamdani's or Chevalier's campaigns, says he is not on any Signal chat with the administration, and describes inviting all three District 13 congressional candidates onto his podcast without payment.
chapters.title: Uptown Voices editor Octavio Blanco denies being paid to cover campaigns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: My name is Octavio Blanco.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: I'm the executive editor of Uptown Voices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: We're a hyperlocal digital news and current events platform based in Washington Heights, Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: We cover Inwood, Washington Heights, Harlem, and the South Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: Thank you for giving me the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: It's important for me to be here to speak about my work and to dispel accusations in the media that we've been paid to cover aspects of Mamdani's or Chevalier's campaigns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: I'm also not on any signal chat with the Mamdani administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: My communications with the administration is via email and phone conversations, sometimes SMS text, as I do with any other source.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: As a digital impact leader in my community, it's very important for me and my publication, Uptown Voices, to retain the tremendous amount of trust that our audience has given us in the 16 months that we've been working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: Trust is our most valuable commodity, and we would never want to threaten that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: Plus, we live in the community and are accountable every day to our neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: That's why during the District 13 congressional race, Uptown Voices made it a point to invite all three candidates to appear on our podcast.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: All the candidates accepted, and each of them appeared twice on our show for one hour each time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: No one paid us to appear on the program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: In fact, in one instance, Adriano Espaillat insisted that we rent a studio to avoid any possible technical difficulties, which we did and paid for out of our own pocket.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: despite having very limited resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: In another instance, the Espayat campaign did offer us a $500 payment to attend a photo op in the community, which we rejected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: I'm proud to say that Uptown Voices punches way above its weight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: We are an accredited news organization with the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: We often attend press conferences and ask sharp questions to the mayor about his policies and plans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: We sit next to our more established national and international and local counterparts, and we ask questions that impact our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: We may be hyper-local, but the issues we face uptown are similar to those faced by people all across the city, country, and dare I say, across the globe as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: I have more to say, but I can't take any questions because I have an interview to go to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: So I will leave that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: I'll leave my comments as those.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have a press pass or you do not press pass?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Octavio Blanco
utterances.text: I do have a press pass.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Charles Diamond, who worked for the city over eight years with procurement expertise, says the city should be suspicious when an agency gets for free what it normally pays for, that zero-dollar contracts are red flags, and that procurement avenues with selection processes and record keeping were not taken.
chapters.title: Charles Diamond raises procurement concerns about city media buying

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: My name is Charles Diamond.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I worked for the city for over eight years, and as you know, I have a particular expertise in procurement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I think that's one angle I want to bring to this that hasn't really been talked about, and then quickly back to the citywide policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: The way that the city buys advertisement, buys media, is a longstanding concern.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: The wonderful doctor in her article spoke with Jose.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Bayona, former head of community and ethnic media.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: And I worked with Jose when we created that new list in the beginning of the Alas administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: It was a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: It was working with DCAS and DOHMH regarding their existing OPAD and Miller contracts in order to figure out a new way to utilize our tools to get the spending the right way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That's called normal government behavior.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: When one person is getting a benefit, we should be very, very, very suspicious when a city agency is getting something for free that they normally pay for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: In fact, it's one of the biggest red flags you can have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: We talk about zero dollar contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Doesn't mean it's not a contract.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: In fact, it should make us more suspicious.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: So clearly here, there are procurement avenues that should have been taken, that could have been taken.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: They chose not to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: What are the benefits of doing that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: A selection process, record keeping, protections against political interference, all of the things that we wanted here today.

chapters.summary: Diamond calls the administration's testimony torturous and its circular logic on transitory versus substantive bewildering, says government business cannot be done on non-approved channels like Signal, questions who approved the app download, and supports Council Member Morano's suggestion of subpoenas.
chapters.title: Diamond criticizes administration's transitory-versus-substantive testimony

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Turning quickly to the process angle, I found the testimony of the administration here before, I mean, torturous to an extreme.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That circular logic behind transitory and substantive, I think was, again, any of us who have worked in the city were bewildered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: What are you telling me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: This is the opposite of everything I've heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Let's be very clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: We all know that you can't do government business on non-approved channels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Signal was not approved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I'd like to give another example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: You can't normally download apps on your phone without IT approving it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Who approved this downloaded app?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Or was it on a private phone?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Was someone ordered to allow that app to be put on there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Councilmember Moreno spoke about subpoenas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I think it's extremely appropriate in this case because, unfortunately, mistakes happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: New people in the city government might not fully get a policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I get that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: But when you go that defensive,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: and you try and pretend that it was okay, it only raises more and more questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Tony Rasan, who runs TBO Harlem Uptown and the Harlem Night Market, says he was part of the Signal group but paid little attention since it mostly contained press links and event notices, that he has never been paid, and that content creators previously lacked access to the mayor's office.
chapters.title: TBO Harlem Uptown's Tony Rasan says he was in the Signal group but unpaid

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: Pleasure being here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: My name is Tony Rasan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: I run TBO Harlem Uptown, and I'm the founder and producer of the Harlem Night Market, as well as the Harlem Wellness Festival.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: We do a lot of work in the community with a special emphasis on amplifying and focusing on small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: Our platform is very popular uptown.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: We have probably one of the largest followings, you know, along with like Uptown Collective and stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: But what I really wanted to kind of come and say and speak and testify in this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: Council hearing is regarding the I guess the the signal group I was a part of that signal group and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: I didn't pay much attention to it because a lot of it is just press stuff like you know links to information or things that that would happen

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: where Mamdani is coming to Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: Those are things that are of particular interest to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: I've refused to, I mean, I just was not interested in some of the things that they kind of put forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: Or, you know, if I see something, a link or something that I'm interested in, I'll reach out and say, hey, I want to be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: But a lot of what I do,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: and the trust in the community that we speak on comes from informing the community about community boards and just to get active in the community to make sure that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: you understand what goes on in terms of like, you know, the biggest problems uptown are affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: I mean, that's among other things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: But one of the things in terms of like our access to City Hall, this is kind of unprecedented because

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: under previous administrations, you know, content creators like myself never really had the opportunity to engage with the mayor's office and other city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: So, you know, that's kind of one of the things that I think is kind of misconstrued.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: I've never been paid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: I don't know people that have been paid, influencers or whatever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: So when I saw the New York Post article, I was kind of confused.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: You know, I laughed about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: A lot of us laughed among ourselves about it because, you know, a lot of this stuff was just not true, what we were reading and stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: I speak for my community, and I speak to my community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: If there's something that I'm not interested in, I don't cover it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: I don't talk about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: And there will be differences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: I already have differences with the Mamdani administration on some of the things that they do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: And I'll talk about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: You know, like, I mean, I'm not, you know, controlled or paid by anybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: Just wanted to say that.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether the material sent to Rasan is similar to what newspapers receive; Rasan says yes, that notices sometimes come the night before events, that he does not get super early access, and that he received public grocery store announcement information like any press outlet, and confirms he does not have a press pass.
chapters.title: Brewer asks Rasan whether Signal content matches what press receives

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One of my questions for you, sir, is I think it's good that this administration is reaching out.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Does it seem like what they're reaching out to you is probably not dissimilar than what they're sending to the Daily News or one of the other newspapers, right?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It seems like it's the same material or not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: Yeah, it is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: And one of the other things, though, like I almost kind of laughed about it, was, you know, sometimes we get notices, you know, literally the night before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: Oh, Mom Donnie's going to be in Harlem, you know, and I'm like, hey, I can't I can't I can't do anything with it because it's just too late on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: You know, you're putting it on my calendar way too late.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: So we're not necessarily getting super early access to information and stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: When he made the announcements on the public grocery stores, I received that information and attended just like any other press outlet would.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have a press pass or you do not?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tony Rasan
utterances.text: I do not have a press pass.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You do not have a press pass.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do not.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks Diamond about the role of media buying middlemen like Miller; Diamond says he relied on subject matter experts like Jose Bayona and Roman Goffman at DCAS, that COVID changed information distribution, and that procurement needed reform to measure outcomes with protections against political interference.
chapters.title: Brewer asks Diamond about media buying middlemen and procurement reform

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have a question about procurement.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Obviously, in this case, it's often the, I call them the middle managers or the millers of the world.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you think that does or doesn't work?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know you didn't have much time, so I wanted to follow up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: No, and I would say as an operations person, I rely on the subject matter expertise of people like Jose Bayona and indeed Roman Goffman at DCAS and saying, how does this work?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I think in terms of it's really evolved and COVID was a big sea change in terms of getting information out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: So again, we talked about meeting people where they are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That's always been the goal in doing that way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I would really say I think procurement wise, it desperately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: needed to be reformed, and we did a great job of reforming that because it was an awful lot of money without necessarily a lot of product.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: But again, I think this is why you want a procurement and selection method with all of the protections that it has because you're measuring outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: What's our goal?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: There's a way of measuring all these things that does indeed sanitize it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: So all in favor of more creative ways of reaching people, but again, we need to do it in the ways that are...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Not violative of other laws that are there for a reason.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: And it really comes down to the idea of, they spoke about it before, people are trained about this all the time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: So either the training didn't happen, or someone ignored it, something happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: And it's especially worrying when it's the mayor's office, because again, as an agency grunt will tell you, the chances of them downloading an app on their phone they're not allowed to have are exactly zero.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: So that is perhaps the worrying part.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you both very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I really appreciate your time.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thanks for waiting.

chapters.summary: Brewer thanks the previous panel and calls the next panel: Tyjuan Green and Norberto Briceño, inviting whoever wants to start.
chapters.title: Brewer calls panel of Tyjuan Green and Norberto Briceño

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Next panel is Taiwan Green and Norbert Briocento.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead, whomever wants to start.

chapters.summary: Tyjuan Green, known as Mr. Fingers, a music producer and community organizer, states he has never been offered or accepted pay for content with the mayor's administration, has lost money covering events, was never directed on messaging, and told the mayor he would hold him accountable.
chapters.title: Content creator Tyjuan Green says he was never paid and holds mayor accountable

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: Thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: My name is Tyjuan Green.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: My handle is Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: Fingers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: I'm a music producer, educator, community organizer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: I would like to state for the record that I have never been offered or accepted to pay for any contact

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: I've done with the mayor administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: In fact, I have lost money from calling out of work to cover events and press conferences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: I was never directed in any way on how to message my videos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: When I was contacted a year ago by a social media team, I still wasn't certain of who I was going to vote for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: After spending time around the then candidate and seeing his consistency every day, I started to believe he could really deliver change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: But that does not mean that I will agree with everything that he does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: I told him and his team I will hold him accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: He told me he wanted to be held accountable and earn the trust of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: They have never stopped me from asking any question, and I have criticized them on some videos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: Why am I doing this for free?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: Because I never thought a person that comes from where I come from would ever have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: the opportunity to have this type of access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: I believe it's my responsibility to sacrifice my time and my resources to educate myself and my followers about the political process and to record and report the full context of stories.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: Traditional press may not have the time to ask questions that are related to Southeast Queens, but I will use this opportunity to do just that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyjuan Green
utterances.text: I have to go.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
